title: The Loyal Mongoose and the Rash Judgment (简体中文)
summary: A gentle couple raises an orphaned mongoose who protects their infant from a venomous snake, teaching generations the eternal lesson of pausing before jumping to false conclusions. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
In a peaceful hamlet nestled between green sugarcane fields lived a gentle village farmer named Devan and his wife Malati. They had a newborn infant son whom they cherished above everything in the world. One rainy morning, Devan found a tiny, shivering orphaned mongoose cub in the woods and brought it home. Malati nursed the little creature with milk and care, and soon the young mongoose grew into a playful, affectionate, and fiercely loyal member of the household.

The mongoose followed Malati everywhere like a gentle puppy, curled up at the foot of their woven cot, and loved watching over the baby's cradle with watchful, amber eyes.

One afternoon, Devan was away working in the distant paddy fields, and Malati needed to fetch water from the village spring. Seeing the infant sleeping peacefully in his cradle and the mongoose dozing guard beside him, Malati whispered: 'Dear little mongoose, watch over our baby until I return with the water pot.' The mongoose blinked softly and rested his chin upon his paws.

While Malati was at the well, a venomous black cobra slithered silently into the cottage through a small opening in the bamboo wall. Sensing the sleeping child, the serpent began gliding toward the cradle.

In a flash, the loyal mongoose sensed danger. His fur stood on end, his eyes flared, and with the courageous instincts of his ancestors, he bounded between the serpent and the cradle! A fierce, desperate battle ensued in the quiet room. The brave mongoose dodged the snake's venomous strikes, lunged forward with razor agility, and after a fierce struggle, defeated the poisonous snake, saving the baby's life. The mongoose lay by the doorway, panting and covered in the dark marks of the struggle.

A few moments later, Malati returned, balancing the brass water pot on her head. As she reached the doorstep, she saw the mongoose lying there with red and dark stains around his mouth.

A surge of blind panic and terror gripped Malati's heart. Without pausing to investigate, without stepping inside to check the cradle, her panicked mind jumped to the most terrible conclusion: *'This animal has harmed my baby!'*

In blind grief and fury, Malati dropped the heavy water pot down upon the little creature. But the moment she rushed past the doorway into the bedroom, she froze in stunned, heart-wrenching realization.

There in the wooden cradle, her baby boy was sleeping peacefully, smiling softly in his dreams. And on the floor right beside the cradle lay the vanquished black serpent, completely neutralized!

Malati gasped and fell to her knees, weeping bitter tears of remorse. 'What have I done? My faithful little guardian saved my child's life, and I judged him without looking with my own eyes!'

Fortunately, in this family retelling, the brave little mongoose was only knocked unconscious by the falling pot. Hearing Malati's cries, Devan rushed home, gently tended to the little creature's bruises with healing herbs, and revived him. Malati embraced the little guardian with tears of gratitude, vowing never again to let blind fear or hasty assumptions cloud her judgment.
moral: 道德启示：Never act in haste or jump to conclusions in moments of anger or panic. Always seek the truth before passing judgment.

title: Tenali Rama and the Cat That Feared Warm Milk (简体中文)
summary: When the King orders every household to feed royal cows' milk to cats to eliminate castle mice, Tenali Rama trains a cat with an amusing aversion to warm milk to make a witty point. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
During the reign of King Krishna Deva Raya in the golden city of Vijayanagara, a sudden plague of field mice invaded the royal granaries, chewing through sacks of rice, barley, and lentils. The King was greatly concerned for the kingdom's food supplies.

To combat the mice, the King ordered that every minister and courtier be given a healthy royal cow and a lively cat. The royal decree announced: 'Every courtier must nourish their cat with fresh, creamy milk drawn daily from their assigned cow. The cats will grow strong, hunt the mice, and protect our food reserves. In one month, all cats will be inspected at the royal palace!'

All the courtiers obeyed. Every day, they fed their cats bowls of warm, fresh milk. The cats grew plump, pampered, and lazy, sleeping on satin cushions in the sun, entirely unbothered by mice.

Tenali Rama also received a beautiful cow and a ginger cat. On the very first morning, Tenali poured boiling hot milk into a copper saucer and placed it before the hungry cat. The poor cat dashed forward and touched the boiling milk with its tongue. *Sssss!* The heat stung its whiskers, and the cat leapt three feet into the air, screeching in fright!

From that day onward, whenever Tenali placed even a bowl of cool, fresh milk before the ginger cat, the animal would arch its back, hiss, and sprint away in terror! Tenali took good care of the cat by feeding it wholesome food and keeping it active, while enjoying the delicious fresh cow's milk with his family and sharing it with poor children in his neighborhood.

At the end of the month, King Krishna Deva Raya summoned all the courtiers with their cats for the grand royal inspection. The courtiers arrived carrying heavy, round, sleeping cats that looked like furry pillows.

Then Tenali Rama stepped forward with his lean, agile, energetic cat.

'Tenali,' remarked the King with a frown, 'your cat looks quite lean. Have you not been feeding him the fresh milk from the royal cow?'

'Your Majesty,' replied Tenali with folded hands, 'my cat refuses to touch milk! He has an intense dread of milk and will not drink even a single drop.'

The King laughed in disbelief. 'A cat that refuses milk? That is impossible! Cats love milk more than anything in the world. Servants, bring a saucer of warm milk immediately!'

The royal servant placed a saucer of warm milk before Tenali's cat. The moment the ginger cat caught the scent of the milk, its fur bristled, its eyes went wide with dread, and it dashed behind Tenali's legs, refusing to go anywhere near the bowl!

The King was utterly astonished. 'Tenali, how can this be? Why does your cat run from milk?'

Tenali Rama bowed with his trademark witty smile: 'Your Majesty, this cat learned on its first day that blindly rushing into luxury can burn your tongue! While the other courtiers stuffed their cats until they became too fat and lazy to catch a single mouse, my cat stayed lean, swift, and sharp. In just four weeks, my cat has cleared our entire street of rodents!'

King Krishna Deva Raya inspected the other cats—every single one was too obese to run after a mouse! The King laughed heartily at Tenali's clever lesson, realizing that excess comfort produces laziness, whereas staying active and mindful keeps both cats and leaders ready for life's challenges.
moral: 道德启示：Excessive luxury and comfort make one complacent and ineffective. True readiness comes from staying active, humble, and disciplined.

title: The Painting of the Magnificent Royal Stallion (简体中文)
summary: When a boastful royal artist mocks the courtiers, King Krishna Deva Raya challenges Tenali Rama to produce a masterpiece. Tenali presents a canvas with only a horse's tail and asks the King to imagine the rest. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
A celebrated artist from a faraway kingdom visited the royal court of Vijayanagara to display his paintings. He showed paintings of sunsets, rolling rivers, and galloping war horses with exquisite detail. King Krishna Deva Raya and all the ministers showered the artist with gold and praise.

The artist became puffed up with arrogance. He sneered at the courtiers: 'None in this court could ever comprehend true art, let alone create a painting of such perfection!'

King Krishna Deva Raya was amused and said, 'Tenali, what do you think of this painting of the warrior?'

Tenali tilted his head and remarked, 'The painting is nice, Your Majesty, but I can only see the front side of the warrior! Where is the other half of his body? And where is the other side of the tree behind him? A truly great artist should show everything!'

The King chuckled: 'Tenali, you know nothing of art! In painting, you must use your imagination to picture what is hidden from view.' Then the King made a playful wager: 'I give you one month and all the paints and canvases you need. Produce a painting as fine as this artist's work, or pay a heavy fine!'

'Challenge accepted, Your Majesty,' Tenali bowed cheerfully.

One month flew by. On the appointed day, the royal court gathered in anticipation. The foreign artist stood near the throne, smirking in expectation of Tenali's humiliation. Tenali Rama entered the grand hall, accompanied by two attendants carrying a massive canvas covered with a heavy velvet cloth.

'Tenali,' the King smiled warmly, 'unveil your masterpiece!'

Tenali pulled off the velvet drape with a flourish. The entire court leaned forward. The large canvas was completely blank, painted a simple grassy green—except for one tiny corner at the very edge, where a curved black and white horse's tail was visible, flicking upward!

King Krishna Deva Raya stared at the canvas, stunned. 'Tenali! What kind of nonsense is this? There is nothing on this canvas except a patch of green and a horse's tail!'

Tenali Rama smiled with serene innocence: 'Ah, Your Majesty, remember what you taught me one month ago? *A true lover of art must use their imagination to picture what is hidden from view!* This is a painting of a magnificent royal stallion. The stallion has just galloped off the edge of the canvas into the lush meadow beyond, and only its noble tail remains visible as it leaps into the distance!'

The courtiers held their breath, nervous about the King's reaction. King Krishna Deva Raya looked at the tail, looked at Tenali's sparkling eyes, and then erupted into roaring laughter that filled the entire palace!

'Touché, Tenali!' cried the King, wiping tears of mirth. 'You used my very own words to defeat my wager!'

The King awarded Tenali a bag of gold coins, while the foreign artist bowed in genuine respect, having learned that true wit and imagination transcend rigid rules of craft.
moral: 道德启示：Humor, imagination, and clever perspective can disarm arrogance and reveal the joy of thinking outside the box.

title: Feed My Fine Silk Coat! (简体中文)
summary: When Mulla Nasruddin is ignored at a wealthy merchant's feast because of his dusty clothes, he returns in an embroidered silk robe and begins feeding pilaf directly into his coat sleeves. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
Mulla Nasruddin was invited to a lavish banquet hosted by the wealthiest nobleman in town. The Mulla had spent the entire morning working diligently in his garden, digging up weeds, pruning grapevines, and planting melon seeds. When the afternoon sun announced the hour of the feast, Nasruddin had no time to change. Dusting the earth from his trousers, he walked straight to the nobleman's grand mansion in his faded cotton tunic and worn sandals.

When Nasruddin arrived, the courtyard was filled with nobles dressed in glistening brocades, gold-trimmed vests, and fragrant perfumes. The servants greeted the wealthy guests with bowing salutations and guided them to the finest silk divans.

But when Nasruddin stepped through the gate, the servants looked at his patched tunic with disdain. No one bowed to him. When Nasruddin greeted his host, the wealthy merchant barely glanced his way, giving only a cold, indifferent nod. When the great feast was served, platters of fragrant saffron pilaf, spiced roast lamb, stuffed grape leaves, and almond sherbet were set before the guests. Nasruddin was seated in the furthest corner behind a pillar, and the servants didn't even offer him a plate!

Nasruddin observed this quietly with a gentle smile. Without saying a word of complaint, he quietly slipped out of the banquet hall and walked back to his humble home.

There, Nasruddin washed himself, combed his beard, and put on his finest garment—a resplendent, shimmering silk coat with gold-embroidered cuffs, a gift given to him years ago by an admiring scholar. He draped a fine turban on his head and returned to the nobleman's mansion.

The moment Nasruddin arrived at the front entrance, the servants gasped in awe. They bowed to the ground, greeted him with musical flutes, and escorted him directly to the head of the banquet table beside the host!

The host rose from his seat, beaming: 'Welcome, honored Mulla Nasruddin! We are graced by your presence! Please partake of our finest dishes!'

A royal platter of steaming saffron rice and delicate pastries was placed before Nasruddin. Everyone watched with reverence to see how the wise teacher would begin.

Nasruddin picked up a handful of warm rice and carefully stuffed it into the pocket of his silk coat. Then he took a spoonful of rich lamb curry and poured it straight down his gold-embroidered sleeve! Next, he dipped the satin edge of his cuff into the bowl of almond sherbet, saying with polite affection: 'Eat, my dear coat, eat! Enjoy the feast! Drink deeply, my fine sleeves!'

The banquet hall went completely silent. The guests dropped their spoons, their eyes wide with disbelief. The host looked bewildered and uncomfortable.

'Mulla-ji!' stammered the host. 'What are you doing? Coats do not eat food! Why are you pouring curry and sherbet onto your beautiful silk garment?'

Mulla Nasruddin wiped his hands calmly with a napkin and addressed the entire hall: 'My dear host, when I came to your house an hour ago as a human being in humble clothes, no one greeted me, no one offered me a seat, and no one gave me a morsel of food. But when I put on this silk coat, you bowed down, seated me at the head of the table, and laid out this magnificent feast. Since it is clear that your hospitality was intended for my clothes and not for me, it is only right that my coat should enjoy the meal!'

The wealthy host turned crimson with shame. He realized how shallow his judgment had been. Falling before Nasruddin, he apologized sincerely to the wise Mulla and to all present, promising that in his house, human beings would forever be honored for their character and heart, never for the garments they wear.
moral: 道德启示：Never judge a person's worth by their outward appearance or clothing. True value lies in character, kindness, and integrity.

title: Searching for the Key Where the Light Is (简体中文)
summary: When neighbors see Mulla Nasruddin crawling under a bright street lamp searching for his lost house key, they are surprised to learn he lost it inside his dark house. A timeless parable on seeking answers where they actually reside. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
On a quiet, starry night in a tranquil village, an old neighbor was walking home when he noticed Mulla Nasruddin on his hands and knees beneath the bright glow of an oil street lamp in the public square. Nasruddin was meticulously sifting through the dust, looking under pebbles and inspecting every blade of grass.

'Good evening, Mulla-ji,' said the neighbor warmly. 'What are you searching for so intently in the dust?'

'Ah, good neighbor,' sighed Nasruddin without looking up, 'I have lost the iron key to my front door! Without it, I cannot enter my home and go to sleep.'

'Do not worry, Mulla! Two pairs of eyes are better than one. I shall help you search.' The kind neighbor got down on his hands and knees beside Nasruddin. Together, they combed through the illuminated circle beneath the lamp, peering into every crevice for nearly half an hour. But the iron key was nowhere to be found.

Puzzled and tired, the neighbor wiped his brow and asked: 'Mulla, are you sure you dropped it right here? Exactly where were you when you lost it?'

Nasruddin pointed casually toward his small, dark cottage sixty paces down the alleyway. 'Oh, I dropped it inside my dark bedroom, near the corner of my wooden trunk!'

The neighbor stared at Nasruddin in utter astonishment, his jaw hanging open. 'You dropped the key inside your bedroom? Then why on earth are we crawling in the dust under this street lamp in the public square?'

Nasruddin looked up with a serene, patient smile: 'Because, my dear friend, it is pitch dark inside my cottage, whereas out here beneath the street lamp, the light is so much better!'

The neighbor burst into laughter, and soon Nasruddin joined in with gentle merriment. But as they walked together with an oil lantern back to the dark cottage, the neighbor realized the profound truth hidden beneath Nasruddin's humorous antics.

How often do human beings search for happiness, peace, and solutions in easy, brightly lit places outside themselves—in possessions, praise, and distractions—when the real answer is hidden inside the quiet, unexplored corners of their own hearts?
moral: 道德启示：Do not search for solutions where it is merely convenient or easy; face the real source of a problem, even if it requires stepping into the dark.

title: The Shepherd Boy Who Cried Wolf (简体中文)
summary: A lonely shepherd boy seeks excitement by repeatedly playing false alarms of a wolf attack, discovering the tragic price of losing the community's trust. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
keywords: trust and honesty fables for kids
full_text:
High on a breezy green hillside bordering a peaceful farming village lived a young shepherd boy named Lucas. Every morning, Lucas drove his flock of fluffy white sheep up the slopes to graze on sweet clover and thyme. His duty was simple but vital: watch the flock, keep them together, and warn the village if any dangerous predator approached from the dark forest.

After several weeks, Lucas grew terribly bored. Day after day, the sun rose, the sheep chewed grass, and the clouds drifted lazily overhead. Nothing exciting ever happened. Lucas longed for company, noise, and excitement.

One afternoon, an irresponsible thought entered his mind: *'What if I play a trick on the villagers? That will bring everyone running!'*

Lucas took a deep breath, ran to the edge of the rocky ridge overlooking the village fields, and screamed at the top of his lungs: 'Wolf! Wolf! A huge gray wolf is attacking the sheep! Help!'

Down in the valley, the villagers dropped their scythes, rakes, and hammers. Fearing for the safety of the boy and their precious flock, they sprinted up the steep hillside, panting with breathless concern. But when they reached the summit, they found no wolf at all—only the sheep grazing peacefully and Lucas rolling on the grass, clutching his belly in roaring laughter.

'That was not funny, Lucas!' warned the village blacksmith sternly. 'A false alarm wastes our labor and frightens everyone. Do not cry wolf when there is no wolf!'

Yet just three days later, overcome once again by boredom, Lucas repeated the prank: 'Wolf! Wolf! Please help, the wolf is here!'

Once more, the kind-hearted villagers hurried up the mountain with sticks and pitchforks to defend him, only to find the boy mocking them with red-faced laughter. The village elder shook his gray head in sorrow: 'Lucas, a liar will not be believed, even when they finally speak the truth.'

A week later, as the twilight shadows lengthened across the hill, a real, terrifying gray wolf crept out from the thick pine forest. Its yellow eyes glowed with hunger, and its sharp teeth bared as it stalked toward a frightened lamb!

Trembling in genuine terror, Lucas scrambled up a tall boulder and screamed with all the strength in his throat: 'Wolf! Wolf! A real wolf is here! Please help me! Wolf!'

Down in the village, the farmers heard the distant cries. But they shook their heads and smiled sadly. 'It is only that mischievous boy trying to trick us again,' said a farmer. 'We will not leave our work to be laughed at a third time.'

No one came to his aid. Lucas could only watch in tears as the wolf scattered the frightened flock into the wild hills. That night, Lucas walked down to the village alone, weeping in deep shame. The villagers comforted him and helped him gather the lost sheep the next morning, but Lucas had learned an unforgettable truth: trust, once broken by deceit, is harder to rebuild than stone.
moral: 道德启示：Truthfulness is the foundation of trust. If you repeatedly tell lies, no one will believe you when you genuinely need help.

title: The Clever Crow and the Stone Pitcher (简体中文)
summary: Parched with thirst under a blazing afternoon sun, a determined crow discovers a tall clay pitcher with water just out of reach, using pebble-by-pebble persistence to solve the problem. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
Under the sweltering heat of a midsummer afternoon, a black crow named Corvus flew across dry fields searching desperately for a drink of water. The streams had dried into cracked mud, and the village animal troughs were bone-dry. Corvus felt his throat parched and his wings heavy with fatigue.

Just as he was about to lose hope, his sharp black eyes spotted an earthen pitcher resting on the stone patio of an abandoned farmhouse garden. Corvus fluttered down and landed eagerly upon the rim of the jug.

He peered inside. To his delight, there was clear, sparkling water at the bottom! But his joy turned to dismay when he stretched his neck downward. The pitcher was tall with a narrow neck, and the water level was low. No matter how much Corvus stretched, his beak stopped two inches short of the water's surface.

He tried to push the heavy clay jar over with his wings, hoping to spill the water onto the flat stones. But the pitcher was made of thick terracotta and filled with too much weight; it stood firm and would not budge. If he knocked it too hard and broke it, the precious water would vanish into the dry soil before he could take a single sip.

Corvus rested on a stone wall, panting. A weaker bird might have given up in despair. But Corvus paused, looked around the garden patio, and used his brilliant mind.

His eyes fell upon a pile of smooth, round pebbles scattered along the gravel path. A spark of scientific inspiration ignited in his bird brain!

Corvus hopped over to the gravel path, picked up a small round pebble in his beak, flew back to the pitcher, and dropped it inside: *Plink!*

He picked up a second pebble and dropped it in: *Plop!*

A third pebble: *Plunk!*

At first, the water level seemed barely to move. It was slow, tedious, and tiring work. But Corvus did not lose heart. He flew back and forth with steady rhythm: pebble by pebble, stone by stone. One, five, ten, twenty, forty pebbles sank to the bottom of the pitcher. With each stone that entered, the water had no choice but to rise higher through displacement.

Finally, after dozens of patient trips, the cool water rose right to the brim of the pitcher! Corvus dipped his black beak into the refreshing water and drank deeply, quenching his thirst in sweet triumph. His patience and ingenuity had saved his life.
moral: 道德启示：Little by little does the trick. Patient, persistent effort and creative thinking can conquer seemingly impossible difficulties.

title: The Gentle Sun and the Boastful North Wind (简体中文)
summary: The blustering North Wind and the radiant Sun hold a contest to see who can persuade a traveler to remove his warm cloak, showing that gentleness achieves what fury never can. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
High above the azure skies, a lively dispute arose between the fierce North Wind and the golden Sun. The North Wind puffed his icy cheeks and roared with thunderous pride: 'I am the mightiest force in all nature! With one blast of my breath, I can snap century-old oak trees, whip the ocean into towering waves, and strip the leaves from entire forests! You, Sun, are merely a soft, warm ball of light. You have no real power!'

The Sun smiled with gentle, calm warmth. 'Strength, dear brother Wind, is not measured only by how loudly you howl or how much destruction you cause. True power lies in gentle persuasion and warmth.'

The North Wind scoffed in disbelief. 'Persuasion? Softness is weakness! Let us have a contest to settle this once and for all.'

Looking down at the earth, the Sun spotted a solitary traveler walking along a winding mountain path. The traveler was wrapped tightly in a thick woolen cloak to protect himself from the autumn chill.

'Look at that traveler,' proposed the Sun. 'Whichever of us can cause that traveler to take off his woolen cloak shall be recognized as the more powerful.'

'A child's play!' boomed the North Wind. 'I shall blow his cloak clean off his shoulders in three seconds. Stand aside and watch!'

The Sun stepped behind a fluffy silver cloud, giving the North Wind first turn.

The North Wind took a tremendous, freezing breath and blew with all his fury: *WHOOOOOSH!* Gusts of icy gale swept down the mountain. Hail and dried leaves spun in violent whirlwinds. The traveler staggered, nearly losing his footing on the rocky ledge.

Did the traveler let go of his cloak? Far from it! The harder and colder the North Wind blew, the tighter the traveler clutched the woolen fabric against his chest, wrapping the edges around his neck and buttoning every clasp securely against the storm!

The North Wind roared in frustration, howling until his lungs were completely exhausted. After fifteen minutes of raging fury, the wind died down to a tired whimper. The traveler remained completely cloaked, shivering but unyielding.

Now it was the Sun's turn.

The Sun emerged gracefully from behind the cloud. He did not roar, demand, or use violence. He simply shone with radiant, steady, affectionate warmth. His golden rays bathed the hillside, the autumn wildflowers, and the winding path in comforting golden light.

Soon, the biting chill evaporated. The birds began singing in the olive groves. The traveler stopped shivering and unclasped the top button of his collar. As the Sun shone a little warmer and brighter, the traveler felt the soothing heat upon his shoulders and back. He wiped a bead of sweat from his forehead.

Finally, feeling wonderfully warm and comfortable, the traveler unbuttoned the cloak, slipped it off his shoulders with a sigh of relief, folded it neatly, and laid it over his arm as he walked merrily forward under the friendly sunshine.

The North Wind hung his head in silent astonishment. The Sun smiled kindly upon his brother: 'You see, dear Wind? Gentleness, warmth, and kind persuasion can accomplish what fury and force can never achieve.'
moral: 道德启示：Gentleness and warmth are far more powerful than fury and force. Kindness opens hearts that harshness only seals shut.

title: The Bremen Town Musicians (简体中文)
summary: Four aging animals—a donkey, a hound, a cat, and a rooster—unite to find a new life of music and dignity, outsmarting bandits with their unforgettable midnight symphony. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
Once upon a time, a hardworking donkey had carried sacks of grain to the mill for many long years. But as his strength waned with old age, his ungrateful master planned to sell him away. Sensation of danger in the air, the clever donkey decided to make his own way in the world. 'I will go to the free city of Bremen,' he thought cheerfully, 'and become a town musician!'

As he trotted along the highway, he found an old hunting hound lying by the roadside, panting wearily. 'Why are you sighing so, old fellow?' asked the donkey.

'Ah,' sighed the hound, 'because I am old and can no longer sprint through the brush to catch foxes, my master wanted to get rid of me. So I ran away, but how shall I earn my bread?'

'Come with me to Bremen!' brayed the donkey warmly. 'I shall play the lute, and you can beat the drums. Together, we shall make grand music!' The hound wagged his tail happily and joined him.

A little further down the road, they met an old ginger cat sitting with a face as gloomy as three rainy days. 'What ails you, whiskered friend?' asked the donkey.

'Now that I am getting gray, my teeth are worn down, and I prefer sitting by the stove purring instead of chasing mice, my mistress wanted to drown me!' wept the cat. 'Where shall I go?'

'You understand night serenades!' said the donkey. 'Join our band and come to Bremen!' The cat beamed and trotted beside them.

Soon, they passed a farmyard where a red rooster was crowing with all his might atop the gate: *Cock-a-doodle-doo!*

'Why are you screeching so loudly?' asked the donkey.

'Guests are coming for Sunday dinner, and the cook plans to put me in the soup pot tonight!' cried the rooster. 'So I am crowing while I still have my throat!'

'Red-comb,' laughed the donkey, 'come with us! Anything is better than the soup pot! You have a magnificent voice; together our quartet will astonish the world!'

By nightfall, the four friends were deep in a dark, whispering forest, still far from Bremen. The donkey and hound curled beneath a large beech tree, while the cat climbed the lower branches, and the rooster flew to the very top.

From the treetop, the rooster called down: 'Friends, I see a cozy warm light glowing through the trees not far away!'

They walked toward the light and discovered a sturdy cottage hidden in the woods. Peering through the illuminated window, the tall donkey saw a table laden with hot roasted potatoes, savory pies, and cider—and around it sat a band of rough robbers celebrating their spoils!

The four friends put their heads together and devised a brilliant plan to drive the robbers away.

The donkey placed his front hooves upon the windowsill. The hound leapt upon the donkey's back. The cat scrambled atop the hound's shoulders. And the rooster flew up and perched proudly upon the cat's head!

At a signal from the donkey, they began their grand symphony together with all their might! The donkey brayed: *HEE-HAW!* The hound barked: *WOOF-WOOF!* The cat meowed: *MEEE-OWWW!* And the rooster screeched: *COCK-A-DOODLE-DOO!* Then they plunged through the windowpane with a tremendous crash of glass!

The terrified robbers leapt from their seats, convinced that a four-headed forest monster had burst through the wall! Screaming in sheer panic, the bandits fled into the pitch-black forest and never dared return.

The four friends laughed with boundless joy. They sat down at the table and feasted upon the delicious pies until their bellies were round. Then they blew out the candles: the donkey slept in the warm straw, the dog behind the door, the cat by the warm hearth, and the rooster atop the roof beam.

They loved their cozy woodland home so dearly that they never needed to journey to Bremen after all, living together in peace, music, and lasting friendship for the rest of their happy days.
moral: 道德启示：Even when others cast you aside, your unique talents and teamwork with loyal friends can create a wonderful new beginning.

title: The Emperor's New Clothes (简体中文)
summary: Two cunning swindlers weave invisible clothes for a vain Emperor, claiming the cloth cannot be seen by anyone unfit for their post. Only an innocent child has the courage to speak the truth. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
keywords: speaking truth to power fairy tale
full_text:
Many years ago, in a grand European capital, lived an Emperor who loved luxurious clothes more than anything else in the world. He did not care for his army, nor for the theatre, nor for caring for the poor; he cared only for parading in magnificent new garments. He had a different coat for every hour of the day.

One day, two cunning swindlers arrived in the city, posing as master weavers from a distant land. They claimed they could weave the most exquisite fabric ever beheld—a cloth whose colors and patterns were of peerless beauty. But its most miraculous quality, they declared, was that the fabric was completely invisible to anyone who was either hopelessly incompetent at their job or utterly stupid!

'Magnificent!' thought the vain Emperor. 'If I wore clothes made of such fabric, I could instantly discover which ministers in my government are unfit for their offices, and I could tell the wise from the foolish! I must have this cloth woven at once!'

The Emperor gave the swindlers large sums of gold and baskets of pure silk and gold thread. The weavers set up two large looms in a royal chamber and pretended to work furiously day and night. But in truth, there was not a single thread upon the empty looms, and they tucked all the gold and silk safely inside their knapsacks!

After a week, the Emperor sent his oldest, most trusted minister to check on the weavers' progress. The old minister entered the room and looked at the looms. His eyes widened in panic: *'Heaven forbid! I cannot see a single thread!'*

'Look at this delicate azure weave!' said one swindler, pointing at the empty air. 'Do you not admire the radiant pattern, Lord Minister?'

The poor minister broke into a cold sweat. *'Am I stupid?'* he thought in dread. *'Am I unfit for my high office? I dare not let anyone know that I see nothing!'* So he nodded enthusiastically: 'Oh, it is breathtaking! The colors! The intricate gold embroidery! I shall tell His Majesty immediately!'

Every courtier and general sent by the Emperor did the exact same thing. No one wanted to appear foolish or incompetent, so everyone praised the invisible cloth to the skies: 'Superb! Magnificent!'

Finally, the grand day arrived. The swindlers held up their empty hands, pretending to drape the Emperor in trousers, coat, and a long royal train. 'Behold, Sire! The garment is as light as a spider's web; you will feel as if you are wearing nothing at all!'

The Emperor posed before his tall mirror, turning this way and that in his underwear, pretending to admire the drape. 'How well it fits! How elegantly it hangs!' he exclaimed nervously, terrified of admitting he was stark naked.

The Emperor marched out into the public square beneath a grand velvet canopy to lead the royal procession. Thousands of citizens lined the streets, waving flags. Everyone had heard of the magic fabric, and no one wanted their neighbors to think they were stupid, so the whole crowd cheered: 'Oh! Look at the Emperor's new clothes! How marvelous! How divine!'

Then, from the front row of the crowd, perched upon her father's shoulders, a little girl tilted her head in confusion. Pointing with her tiny finger, she called out in a clear, sweet voice that echoed over the cheering:

*'But he isn't wearing anything at all!'*

A stunned silence fell over the square. The father blushed and whispered, 'Listen to the innocent child!' Then one neighbor whispered to another: 'The child says he has no clothes on!'

'He has no clothes on!' whispered someone else. And suddenly, the whole crowd of thousands of people erupted into a roar of laughter: *'He isn't wearing anything at all!'*

The Emperor shivered. He realized in his burning heart that the child was speaking the honest truth! But he was too proud to stop. So he held his head higher than ever, and his noble chamberlains walked behind him, diligently carrying a royal train that did not exist at all, while the honest truth echoed freely through the sunny streets.
moral: 道德启示：It takes genuine courage to speak the truth when everyone else is pretending. Never let the fear of what others think silence your honesty.

title: The Secret of the King's Royal Brinjals (简体中文)
summary: When the King guards a rare purple vegetable with high palace walls, Tenali Rama's wife desires a taste. Tenali devises an ingenious dream play to protect his young son from telling a lie. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
In the royal botanical garden of Vijayanagara, King Krishna Deva Raya cultivated a rare variety of brinjal (eggplant). The vegetables were deep violet, extraordinarily sweet, and guarded day and night by armed royal sentries. No citizen was permitted to pick or taste even a single leaf under penalty of severe punishment.

One evening, the King hosted a small dinner for his closest ministers and served a curry prepared from the royal brinjals. Tenali Rama was enchanted by its rich, succulent flavor. When he returned home, he spoke so poetically about the delicious dish that his wife, Sharada, longed to prepare it for their young son, little Ramu.

'Can you not bring just two brinjals from the royal garden?' pleaded Sharada. 'Our child has never tasted such a delicacy.'

Tenali hesitated. Stealing royal produce was treason, but seeing his wife's pleading eyes, he made up his mind to pluck two brinjals under moonlight. Scaling the palace garden wall with agile footwork, he plucked two ripe brinjals and slipped home unnoticed. Sharada cooked a fragrant, mouthwatering curry and fed it to little Ramu, who ate with round-eyed joy.

However, Tenali realized a serious danger: Ramu was only six years old and innocent. Children speak whatever comes to their minds. If the palace guards came inquiring, Ramu would innocently say, 'I ate royal brinjals for dinner!'

Tenali smiled and whispered a plan to his wife.

That night, while Ramu was sound asleep on his woven cot, Tenali gently carried the sleeping boy up to the flat rooftop. Clouds drifted across the dark sky, and a gentle night breeze blew. Tenali splashed water droplets over the roof tiles, scooped handfuls of water from a copper jug and let them trickle over the boy's face and arms, while shaking a thin sheet of metal to make low, rumbling sounds: *Rumble, rumble, whoosh! Splash!*

'Wake up, Ramu!' shouted Tenali playfully. 'A wild thunderstorm has broken out! Look at the heavy rain and lightning on the roof!'

The sleepy boy blinked in the darkness, feeling cold water on his brow and hearing the rumbling metal. Tenali then carried him down into the dry bedroom, tucked him under a warm quilt, and let him drift back into peaceful sleep.

The next morning, the head palace gardener discovered two brinjals missing and reported the theft to King Krishna Deva Raya. The King was furious: 'Who dared trespass in my garden? Search every minister's house!'

Soon, royal guards knocked on Tenali Rama's door. 'Tenali, did your household eat royal brinjals last night?'

'Certainly not!' declared Tenali. 'Search our kitchen.' The guards found only rice and lentil soup.

Then the guard chief saw little Ramu playing in the courtyard with clay marbles. 'Come here, little one,' asked the chief kindly. 'What did you have for dinner last night?'

Ramu smiled brightly: 'I ate the most delicious royal brinjal curry with hot rice!'

The guard turned triumphantly to Tenali: 'Aha! The innocent child has spoken the truth! Arrest Tenali Rama!'

Tenali calmly shook his head. 'Wait, officer. Ask the boy what else happened last night before making an arrest.'

The guard turned back to Ramu: 'Tell us what happened after dinner, little boy.'

Ramu's eyes went wide with wonder: 'After dinner, my father and I went up to the rooftop in the middle of the night, and there was a huge thunderstorm! Gallons of rain poured over my head, thunder rumbled across the sky, and lightning flashed across the roof tiles!'

The guard chief blinked in utter disbelief. He looked at the sky and out at the sunny village square. 'Thunderstorm? Heavy rain last night? The skies were crystal clear, with not a single cloud in all of Vijayanagara!'

The guards burst out laughing. 'The poor child is confusing his dreams with reality! He had a vivid dream of eating royal brinjals while dreaming of a rooftop storm!'

The guards apologized and left without making an arrest. When King Krishna Deva Raya heard the guard's report, he saw through the trick, smiled at Tenali's psychological genius, and gifted Tenali a whole basket of royal brinjals with a playful warning never to climb the garden wall again.
moral: 道德启示：A sharp mind understands how memory, innocence, and perception work. Love and wit can protect family while preserving innocent hearts.

title: The Golden Mangoes and the Hot Iron Ladle (简体中文)
summary: When greedy priests take advantage of the King's grief by demanding solid gold mangoes, Tenali Rama uses a sizzling iron spoon to teach a humorous lesson in genuine devotion versus greed. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
King Krishna Deva Raya was deeply devoted to his elderly mother, the Queen Mother Nagala Devi. In her final days, the Queen Mother fell ill and expressed a gentle dying wish: 'My son, I have a sudden longing to taste a sweet, ripe Alphonsa mango.'

The King immediately sent attendants to find ripe mangoes across the kingdom. But it was late winter, and mango trees were barely in blossom. Before the fruit could be brought from a distant province, the gentle Queen Mother passed away peacefully.

The King was overwhelmed by grief and remorse. He blamed himself for failing to fulfill his mother's final wish. Seeing the King's vulnerable sorrow, a group of greedy court priests approached the throne with deceitful advice.

'O King,' whispered the chief priest gravely, 'your beloved mother's spirit cannot find rest unless her final desire is honored. You must cast twenty-one life-sized mangoes crafted from pure, solid gold and donate them to us priests in charity. Only then will her soul attain eternal peace!'

The sorrowful King agreed without hesitation and ordered the royal goldsmiths to forge twenty-one heavy mangoes of pure gold.

When Tenali Rama heard of this exploitation, he was deeply indignant. The priests were playing upon the King's emotional grief to enrich themselves with thousands of gold sovereigns! Tenali decided to intervene with poetic justice.

The day before the royal donation ceremony, Tenali Rama sent a humble invitation to the very same twenty-one priests: 'Tomorrow morning, before you visit the royal palace, please come to Tenali's house. I too wish to make a sacred donation in memory of my late mother.'

The greedy priests were ecstatic: *'Ah! Two donations in one day! We shall be wealthy beyond measure!'*

Early the next morning, the twenty-one priests arrived at Tenali's courtyard, wearing ceremonial robes and chanting mantras with wide smiles. Tenali greeted them with folded hands, offered them silver bowls of cool water, and then locked the courtyard iron gate behind them.

From the courtyard fire-pit, Tenali picked up a long iron ladle whose curved end was glowing red-hot from the charcoal embers!

The priests jumped back in alarm. 'Tenali! What in heaven's name are you doing with that red-hot branding ladle?'

Tenali bowed with mournful eyes: 'Venerable priests, my beloved late mother suffered from severe joint aches and rheumatism in her final years. Her dying wish was to be treated with the warmth of a heated iron spoon on her knees. Alas, she passed before I could soothe her ache! Therefore, to grant her spirit peace, I must apply this red-hot iron ladle to the knees of all twenty-one of you!'

The priests turned white with horror! 'Are you insane, Tenali?' shouted the chief priest, backing into the locked gate. 'Branding our legs with hot iron will cause us agony! What has that got to do with your mother's soul?'

Tenali looked at them with serene innocence: 'Honored priests, if giving solid gold mangoes to your hands can satisfy the appetite of the King's mother in heaven, surely pressing a hot ladle to your legs will soothe the aching knees of my mother in heaven!'

The priests were caught in their own hypocritical web. They realized that their greedy scheme had been exposed. Trembling in panic, they pleaded: 'Tenali, spare us! We confess our greed! We will never ask for the King's golden mangoes!'

Tenali opened the courtyard gate. The priests sprinted out into the street as fast as their legs could carry them, never looking back.

When King Krishna Deva Raya learned what had transpired, his eyes were opened to the priests' selfish manipulation. He canceled the wasteful donation, embraced Tenali in profound gratitude, and distributed the gold instead as charity to build hospitals, orphanages, and schools for the poor.
moral: 道德启示：Greed that exploits human grief and love is shameful. True honor to ancestors is shown through genuine compassion, charity, and helping the living.

title: The Golden Swan and the Cost of Greed (简体中文)
summary: A benevolent golden swan sheds a single golden feather each week to support a poor widow and her daughters, until greed overtakes gratitude with irreversible consequences. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
Long ago, in a tranquil valley bordered by sandalwood groves, lived a poor widow named Sujata and her two gentle daughters. They lived in a humble thatch-roofed cottage, spinning cotton thread from dawn till dusk to earn enough copper coins for a simple bowl of rice.

Near their cottage was a clear, crystal lake where a magnificent swan made his home. This was no ordinary swan; he had brilliant, shimmering golden plumage that glowed like morning sunlight upon water. The swan possessed great compassion and wisdom.

Seeing Sujata and her daughters working until their fingers were sore, the golden swan felt deep sympathy in his heart. 'I must help this kind family without making them dependent upon charity,' he mused.

One evening, the swan flew to their cottage porch. Sujata and the girls looked in wonder as the radiant bird spoke in a gentle, melodic voice: 'Good mother, do not weep over your poverty. Once every week, I shall visit your porch and shed a single golden feather from my wing. You may sell the feather in the town market, and the gold will provide ample food, warm clothes, and schoolbooks for your children.'

With a gentle flap of his wings, the swan shed one gleaming feather of pure solid gold upon the wooden threshold, then flew back to his lake.

Sujata sold the feather the next morning. The jeweler paid her a handsome sum. For the first time in years, the family had fresh milk, warm blankets, and nutritious vegetables. True to his word, the golden swan returned every seven days, gifting a single golden feather each time. The family's debt vanished, their home was repaired, and the daughters flourished in their studies.

However, as the months passed, a dark, creeping greed began to take root in Sujata's heart. She looked at the cozy home and thought: *'What if the swan flies away across the mountains one day and never returns? Why should we wait week after week for a single feather? If I pluck all his feathers at once, we shall be wealthy for ten generations!'*

Her elder daughter protested with tears in her eyes: 'Mother! The swan is our kindest benefactor! He gives freely from his heart. To harm him or take by force would be cruel and ungrateful!'

Sujata dismissed her daughter's wise plea. The following week, when the golden swan landed gently on the porch, Sujata greeted him with honeyed words. As the unsuspecting swan bowed his neck to shed his feather, Sujata seized him firmly by both wings!

The terrified swan struggled, but Sujata ruthlessly plucked every single feather from his wings and body. But the moment the feathers were ripped from the bird's flesh against his will, a miraculous transformation occurred: the golden feathers turned instantly into ordinary, dull white goose feathers in her grasping hands!

Sujata gasped in horror, dropping the coarse white feathers upon the floor. The naked, shivering swan rested on the porch, his eyes filled with profound sorrow, not anger.

The daughters wept and gently carried the shivering bird to a soft nest of dry straw, feeding him grain and nursing his wounds with medicinal oils. Over many weeks, the swan's feathers grew back—not as brilliant gold, but as pure, soft, ordinary white feathers.

As soon as his wings were fully healed, the swan spread his white plumage and took flight into the endless blue sky, never to visit that porch again. Sujata lived the rest of her days in deep remorse, having learned that greed destroys the very blessings that patience and gratitude preserve.
moral: 道德启示：Gratitude preserves blessings; greed destroys them. Contentment with what is freely given brings lasting joy.

title: The Monkey King and the River Bridge (简体中文)
summary: When a human king's archers surround an ancient mango grove, the noble Monkey King uses his own body as a living bridge across a roaring chasm so every member of his tribe can escape to safety. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
High along the rocky banks of the sacred River Ganga stood a colossal wild mango tree. Its roots sank deep into the riverbed, its leaves shone like emeralds, and its branches were heavy with sweet, golden fruit whose aroma wafted across the entire valley. In this magnificent tree lived a tribe of eighty thousand wild monkeys, led by a wise, strong, and deeply compassionate Monkey King.

The Monkey King had always instructed his tribe with caution: 'Eat only the fruit that hangs over the forest floor. Never let a single ripe mango drop into the flowing river, for if it floats downstream to human settlements, men will discover our sanctuary and bring danger.'

For many years, the monkeys obeyed carefully. But one day, a single ripe mango, hidden behind a bird's nest, dropped into the swift current and floated downstream. It washed ashore near the royal bathing pavilion of the King of Varanasi.

The King's royal cooks discovered the magnificent fruit. When the King tasted its divine sweetness, he declared: 'Find the tree that bears such fruit at once! I must possess it!'

The King's royal flotilla sailed upriver following the fragrance until they arrived beneath the giant mango tree. Seeing eighty thousand monkeys leaping in the branches, the King ordered his archers to surround the tree at nightfall. 'Surround the perimeter! When dawn breaks, shoot all the monkeys so we can claim the entire harvest!'

The monkeys huddled in terror. Chattering in panic, mothers held their babies, knowing that the river rushed violently below and armed human soldiers blocked the forest behind.

The Monkey King leapt to the highest bough and saw their only hope: on the opposite bank of the roaring river, beyond the reach of human arrows, stood a tall bamboo grove. But the river was wide, and no monkey could leap across such a dizzying chasm.

Without hesitating for a second, the Monkey King took a long, flexible bamboo reed, tied one end firmly around his sturdy ankle, and launched his body across the roaring canyon in a magnificent leap of faith! He gripped the outstretched branch of a banyan tree on the safe bank with both hands.

Alas! The bamboo stalk was three feet too short! The brave Monkey King stretched his arms, shoulders, and chest to their absolute limit. Clamping his fingers around the banyan branch with iron resolve, his own body bridged the remaining gap across the roaring abyss.

'Cross!' called the Monkey King in a clear, loving command. 'Run across my back to safety! Quickly, before dawn breaks!'

One by one, the monkeys hesitated, then sprinted across the taut bamboo stalk and over the back of their beloved leader into the safe grove. Mothers carrying tiny babies, elderly monkeys, and playful youths trotted across his spine: eighty thousand animals crossing to freedom.

The strain upon the Monkey King's muscles, tendons, and joints was agonizing. Yet through every agonizing minute, he held on with unbroken love, refusing to let go until the very last baby monkey had stepped safely onto the grass.

The human King of Varanasi had watched this breathtaking spectacle through the moonlight in stunned awe. He had never seen such noble, selfless leadership in all his life. Deeply moved, the human King ordered his men to lower their bows and spread a soft linen net to catch the exhausted Monkey King as he finally released his grip and fell from the branch.

The King personally cradled the noble animal, washed his brow with fragrant rose water, and asked in reverent wonder: 'You are their king. Why did you risk your life and endure such torment for common monkeys?'

The Monkey King opened his gentle eyes and whispered with peaceful dignity: 'Sire, a true ruler is not someone who sits on a throne demanding service from others. A true ruler is a servant and guardian who offers their own strength to lift their people to safety.'

With these parting words of profound wisdom, the Monkey King rested peacefully, healed by the King's royal physicians. From that day forward, the King of Varanasi proclaimed the sacred mango forest an eternal sanctuary for all wild creatures, forever remembering the living bridge of love.
moral: 道德启示：True leadership is rooted in love, service, and sacrifice. The greatest leaders use their strength not to dominate, but to protect and uplift others.

title: The Frog Prince and the Well of Promises (简体中文)
summary: When a young princess drops her golden ball into a deep forest spring, a talking frog retrieves it on one condition: that she keep her word and treat him as a friend. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
In olden times, when wishes still held power, lived a King whose youngest daughter was admired across the realm for her cheerful laughter. Near the King's castle stood a vast, shadowy forest, and under an ancient linden tree in the forest lay a deep, crystal-cool spring.

On hot summer afternoons, the young princess loved walking into the cool shade of the forest. Her favorite plaything was a heavy golden ball. She would toss the gleaming sphere high into the sunlit air and catch it with her nimble hands.

One afternoon, she threw the golden ball so high that her hands missed it as it fell. The ball bounced against the mossy flagstones, rolled over the rim of the spring, and sank down into the deep, dark water. The spring was so deep that no eye could see the bottom. The princess sat upon the stones and wept bitterly.

Suddenly, a thick, croaking voice broke the silence: 'Why do you weep so bitterly, royal maiden? Your tears could melt even a stone.'

The princess looked up and saw an ugly green frog with bulging eyes poking his head above the water lilies. 'Ugh, you clumsy water-paddler!' she sniffed. 'I weep because my beautiful golden ball has fallen into the deep spring.'

'Do not weep,' replied the frog kindly. 'I can dive down and retrieve your golden treasure. But what will you give me if I bring it back?'

'Whatever you ask, dear frog!' cried the princess eagerly. 'My silk dresses, my pearl necklaces, even the golden crown upon my head!'

The frog shook his head gently: 'I have no need for your dresses, pearls, or golden crowns. But if you will love me, let me be your companion and playmate, let me sit at your table, eat from your golden plate, and sleep in your cozy bed—if you promise me this, I will dive down and bring you the ball.'

'Yes, yes, I promise you everything you wish!' cried the princess. But in her secret heart, she thought: *'What nonsense that silly frog talks! He belongs in the pond with his fellow croakers; how could he ever be a companion to a human princess?'*

Trusting her word, the frog dipped his head beneath the water, swam down into the murky depths, and a moment later surfaced with the gleaming golden ball in his mouth. He tossed it onto the soft moss.

The princess shrieked with joy! She snatched up the golden ball and sprinted back toward the castle as fast as her slippers could carry her.

'Wait! Wait!' croaked the frog from the water. 'Take me with you! I cannot run as fast as you!' But the princess did not turn around; she rushed inside the castle gates and forgot the poor creature completely.

The next evening, as the royal family sat at the grand marble dinner table, a wet, pattering sound came up the marble staircase: *Plip, plop, plip, plop!* Then came a gentle knock at the heavy carved door: 'Youngest princess, open the door for me!'

The princess ran to open the door, but when she saw the green frog sitting on the doormat, she slammed the door shut and hurried back to her chair, pale and trembling.

The King noticed her distress. 'My child, what has frightened you so? Is there a giant outside?'

'No, father,' she confessed in embarrassment. 'It is only a slimy green frog.' She explained how she had dropped her golden ball into the spring and made a promise to the creature, never expecting he could ever leave his pond.

Just then, the knock sounded again: *'Youngest daughter of the King, remember the word you gave by the spring!'*

The wise King looked at his daughter with firm, loving eyes: 'My daughter, that which you have promised in your hour of need, you must faithfully perform. Go at once, open the door, and invite him in.'

The princess bowed her head in shame. She opened the door, and the frog hopped inside, following her to her chair. He ate politely from her plate, and though the princess was hesitant at first, she noticed how gentle, considerate, and well-spoken the frog was.

When bedtime arrived, the King gently reminded her of her promise. The princess picked up the frog with two careful fingers and placed him gently upon a soft velvet pillow beside her bed. 'Thank you, kind princess,' whispered the frog softly. 'You have honored your word.'

As the first golden rays of dawn shone through the stained-glass window, a wondrous transformation occurred: the frog's rough green skin fell away, and in his place stood a handsome, gentle prince with smiling eyes! He had been placed under a bitter spell by an unkind sorceress, doomed to remain a beast until a princess honored her promise of companionable kindness.

The prince and princess became lifelong companions, ruling their realm with fairness, honesty, and an enduring respect for promises made to all living beings.
moral: 道德启示：A promise given must be faithfully kept, regardless of circumstances. Never judge others by their appearance, for true nobility is found in loyalty and kindness.

title: The Golden Goose and the Simple Heart (简体中文)
summary: When a generous boy shares his humble bread with a hungry gray traveler, he is gifted a goose with pure golden feathers that brings laughter and joy to an entire sorrowful kingdom. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
In a quiet woodland village lived three brothers. The youngest was nicknamed Dummling, not because he lacked wit, but because he was quiet, unassuming, and never pushed himself forward. His older brothers were boastful, selfish, and frequently mocked Dummling for his gentle nature.

One morning, the eldest brother went into the forest to chop firewood. His mother packed him a rich almond cake and a jug of sweet apple cider. In the woods, an old gray traveler approached him and asked: 'Good youth, please give me a small crust of your cake and a sip of your drink, for I am faint with hunger.' But the selfish brother sneered: 'If I share with you, there will be less for me! Begone!' The selfish youth struck a tree clumsily with his axe and nicked his arm, returning home in pain.

The next day, the second brother went into the forest with a sweet pastry. When the same old traveler asked for a morsel, the second brother replied coldly: 'What I give to you is lost to me!' He swung his axe carelessly, injured his ankle, and hobbled home empty-handed.

On the third morning, Dummling said to his father: 'Father, let me go and chop firewood.' His father scoffed, but Dummling persisted. His mother gave him only a dry crust of barley bread baked in the ashes and a bottle of sour water.

In the forest, the old gray traveler appeared and said: 'Kind boy, give me a morsel to eat and a drop to drink; I am hungry and thirsty.'

Dummling smiled with open warmth: 'I have only dry ash-bread and sour water, but if that pleases you, sit down with me on this fallen log and let us share it with glad hearts.'

They sat together. But when Dummling opened his cloth, lo and behold! The ash-bread had turned into a fresh, warm honey cake, and the sour water had become rich, sparkling apple cider! They ate and drank together in joyful fellowship.

When they finished, the old traveler said with a twinkle in his eye: 'Because you have a generous heart and gladly shared your bread, I will grant you good fortune. Cut down that ancient oak tree over yonder, and you will find a treasure among its roots.'

Dummling cut down the oak tree. Nestled in a hollow beneath the mossy roots was a goose whose feathers were made of pure, sparkling, solid gold! Dummling tucked the golden bird under his arm and walked toward the town inn to rest for the night.

At the inn, the innkeeper had three daughters. Seeing the golden goose, the eldest daughter thought: *'I must have just one of those golden feathers!'* When Dummling looked away, she reached out to pluck a feather. But the moment her fingers touched the goose, her hand stuck fast! Her second sister rushed to pull her away, and her hands stuck fast to her sister's skirt! The third sister cried out, ran forward, and her hands stuck to the second sister!

The next morning, Dummling picked up his golden goose and strolled cheerfully toward the royal city, entirely unconcerned that the three sisters were compelled to trot behind him in a comical single file!

Along the highway, the village pastor shouted: 'For shame, girls! Let go of that youth!' He grabbed the youngest girl's sleeve, and he too was stuck! The parish clerk ran to pull the pastor, and two farmers joined to help, until a hilarious parade of seven people were trotting, tumbling, and stumbling behind Dummling and his golden goose across the countryside!

Now, in the royal capital lived a King whose only daughter suffered from such profound melancholy that she had not smiled or laughed in ten long years. The King had proclaimed that whoever could make the princess laugh would be honored with royal favor and great wealth.

Dummling entered the city gates with his bizarre, hopping procession: seven people tethered like human dominoes, tripping over wheelbarrows, stepping into puddles, and shouting apologies in chorus! When the sad princess looked out from the palace balcony and saw this absurd, comical circus tumbling past, her sorrow melted away. She burst into a fountain of hearty, ringing laughter that echoed across the entire square!

The King was overjoyed. He had the sticky spell released, rewarded the innkeeper's daughters and farmers with silver for their unwitting performance, and warmly embraced Dummling. Dummling was appointed Royal Counselor of Welfare, ensuring that no traveler in the kingdom ever went hungry again.
moral: 道德启示：Generosity and sharing what little you have opens the door to unexpected blessings. A joyful, humble heart brings light to those trapped in sorrow.

title: The Star Talers and the Generous Heart (简体中文)
summary: A gentle orphan girl gives away her bread, her cap, her jacket, and her dress to poor shivering travelers in the cold woods, until the night sky showers her with shining golden stars. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
Once upon a time, there was a little orphan girl whose father and mother had passed away. She was so poor that she no longer had a room to sleep in, nor a bed to lie upon, and nothing in the world except the clothes she wore upon her back and a single crust of bread in her little apron pocket.

Yet, despite her poverty, she was good, gentle, and had a heart overflowing with trust and kindness.

Since she had no home left in the village, she walked out into the countryside, trusting that the world would guide her steps. Along the woodland path, she met a poor old man who leaned heavily upon a crooked willow cane. 'Oh, kind child,' he whispered, shivering, 'give me something to eat; I am so hungry!'

The girl reached into her apron pocket and gave him the whole crust of bread. 'May it nourish you and bring you strength, grandfather,' she said with a warm smile, and walked on.

A little further on, she met a small child crying by the roadside. 'My head is so cold, so cold!' wept the child. Without hesitating, the girl took off her own warm woolen cap, placed it tenderly upon the child's head, and kissed her cheek.

A bit further on, she met another shivering child who had no jacket in the biting autumn breeze. The girl took off her own warm jacket and gave it to the child, saying: 'Wear this, little brother, and keep warm.'

At twilight, she entered a dark, whispering pine forest. There she met yet another child who had no shirt and begged for a covering. The good girl thought to herself: *'It is dark night now, and no one can see me in the forest; this poor child needs my dress far more than I do.'* So she slipped off her little dress and gave that away too, standing in the quiet clearing wearing only her simple cotton slip.

Now she had nothing left in the entire world—no bread, no cap, no jacket, and no dress. She stood alone in the peaceful forest beneath the canopy of ancient pines.

Suddenly, as the evening bells chimed softly in the distant village, the deep indigo sky illuminated with radiant, sparkling light. Falling from the heavens like gentle silver rain came thousands of sparkling stars—and as they touched the mossy earth, each star transformed into a gleaming silver taler coin of pure, precious metal!

And behold! The simple cotton slip she wore was miraculously spun into the finest, softest, shimmering linen dress, glowing with the warmth of summer morning sunlight!

The gentle girl gathered the fallen star coins into her lap. She was rich now—not only with silver coins to provide warmth, food, and shelter for all the poor children and orphans of the valley for all their days, but rich in a heart that had given everything with unreserved love.
moral: 道德启示：Generosity without expectation is the highest form of grace. Those who give freely of their heart will always find the universe sheltering them in return.

title: The Little Fir Tree in the Pine Woods (简体中文)
summary: A young fir tree spends all his days longing for future grandeur, failing to appreciate the warm sunshine, singing birds, and morning dew around him, until he learns the timeless value of living in the present. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
Out in the deep, fragrant woods stood a pretty little fir tree. It occupied a lovely spot with plenty of fresh mountain air and warm sunlight, surrounded by tall companions—towering pines and graceful spruces. Yet the little fir tree was not at all happy.

It did not care for the warm golden sunbeams that caressed its green needles. It did not care for the sweet mountain breeze that whispered through the leaves. When village children wandered through the woods with baskets filled with wild strawberries, they would sit near the little tree and say: 'Look at this darling little fir! How pretty and green it is!'

The little tree hated being called 'little.' It sulked and thought: *'Oh, if only I were a tall, majestic tree like the others! Then I could spread my branches wide across the sky, look out over the wide world, and have eagles build their nests in my highest boughs!'*

In the winter, when the snow lay white and glittering like diamonds upon the forest floor, a swift hare would often come leaping past and jump right over the little tree. Oh, how that annoyed him! *'To be so tiny that even a rabbit can hop over my head!'* he fumed.

'Rejoice in your youth!' sang the warm sunbeams. 'Rejoice in your fresh new needles and the sweet sap flowing through your branches!'

And the whispering wind kissed the little tree, and the morning dew wept sparkling tears upon it, but the fir tree understood neither the breeze nor the dew. It wanted only to be tall, to be somewhere else, to become something grander in the future.

Two winters passed, and the little fir had grown so tall that the hare had to run around it. Yet still the tree sighed: *'Growing is not enough! I want to be chopped down and made into the tall mast of a magnificent sailing ship that travels across stormy oceans!'*

When autumn came, woodcutters arrived in the forest. They felled some of the tallest, oldest pine trees with heavy thuds. The little fir tree trembled with mixed fear and longing. A swallow told him that ships across the sea had tall wooden masts that looked splendid and smelled like pine resin.

Then came Christmas Eve. Woodcutters walked through the groves and selected the little fir tree itself, cutting its trunk cleanly. It was carried into a grand mansion, placed in a brass tub filled with sand, and decorated with silk ribbons, gilded apples, walnuts wrapped in silver foil, and dozens of glowing wax candles! At the very top, a golden star sparkled.

That evening, children danced around the tree in pure enchantment. The candles flickered, and the children laughed and sang songs. The fir tree felt proud: *'Now my true glory has arrived!'*

Yet when morning came, the candles were put out. Attendants dismantled the toys and carried the dry tree up into a dark attic corner. The little tree stood alone in the shadows, listening to the dust settle.

In the quiet dark of the attic, the little fir tree finally began to think deeply with an open heart. It remembered the warm sunbeams of the forest. It remembered the gentle mountain breezes. It remembered the songbirds that had sung in its branches and the playful hare leaping over the snow.

*'How beautiful was the forest!'* whispered the tree with a tender sigh of gratitude. *'How sweet was the morning dew! If only I had rejoiced in the glorious sunshine while I had it, instead of constantly wishing my days away!'*

In this gentle bedtime retelling, a kind gardener finds the fir tree in the spring, plants its root-ball in the sunny earth of the castle meadow, and water brings it back to life. The grateful fir tree lives on for a hundred peaceful years, savoring every single drop of rain, every warm sunbeam, and every breeze that caresses its fragrant needles.
moral: 道德启示：Do not spend your days wishing for the future or longing to be somewhere else. Savor and appreciate the beauty, family, and joy of the present moment.

title: The Cooking Pot That Gave Birth and Passed Away (简体中文)
summary: When a greedy neighbor lends Mulla Nasruddin a copper cooking pot, Nasruddin returns it with a tiny pot claiming it gave birth. When the neighbor happily accepts, Nasruddin prepares the ultimate lesson in poetic justice. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
Mulla Nasruddin had a neighbor named Kasim who was notoriously greedy, selfish, and cunning. Kasim was always eager to take from others, but would never lend a single grain of wheat without demanding interest.

One evening, Nasruddin knocked on Kasim's door. 'Good neighbor Kasim,' said Nasruddin with a humble bow, 'I am preparing a large feast for traveling scholars tonight. Could you please lend me your large copper cooking cauldron for just one day? I shall return it safely tomorrow.'

Kasim hesitated, but seeing a chance to place Nasruddin in his debt, he brought out his heavy copper pot. 'Take it, Mulla. But return it tomorrow without a scratch!'

The next morning, Nasruddin brought the copper cauldron back to Kasim's house. Inside the large pot was a brand-new, tiny copper saucepan.

Kasim inspected the pot and saw the little saucepan. 'Mulla, what is this tiny saucepan doing inside my cauldron?'

Nasruddin beamed with joyful congratulations: 'Rejoice, neighbor Kasim! Last night, while resting in my kitchen, your large cooking pot gave birth to this adorable baby pot! Since the mother pot belongs to you, the baby pot naturally belongs to you as well!'

Kasim stared at Nasruddin. He knew that copper pots do not give birth—that was scientifically impossible! But his insatiable greed whispered: *'Why argue? I am getting a free copper saucepan for nothing!'*

So Kasim smiled broadly and patted Nasruddin on the shoulder: 'How wonderful! Thank you, wise Mulla! Your honesty is commendable!' Kasim gleefully took both pots inside his kitchen.

Two weeks later, Nasruddin visited Kasim again: 'Dear neighbor Kasim, I have another feast tonight. Could you please lend me your large copper cauldron once more?'

Kasim was ecstatic: *'Perhaps it will give birth to twins this time!'* He brought out his finest, heaviest copper cauldron with both hands and handed it to Nasruddin with an eager grin.

One day passed. Then two days. Then a whole week went by, but Nasruddin did not return the pot.

Unable to contain his impatience, Kasim marched over to Nasruddin's house and pounded on the wooden door: 'Nasruddin! Where is my cauldron? Why have you not brought it back?'

Nasruddin opened the door slowly. His eyes were downcast, his shoulders slumped, and he wiped away an imaginary tear with the sleeve of his tunic.

'Alas, my dear brother Kasim!' sighed Nasruddin mournfully. 'I bring you tragic and sorrowful news. Yesterday afternoon, with no warning whatsoever... your beloved copper cauldron passed away! It is dead!'

Kasim turned purple with rage. 'Dead? Are you out of your mind, Nasruddin? How can a copper cooking pot die? Pots are made of metal; they do not have lungs, blood, or life! You are lying to steal my cauldron!'

Mulla Nasruddin looked calmly into Kasim's raging eyes with an amused, serene smile:

'My dear neighbor Kasim, you were perfectly willing to believe that a copper pot could be alive when it gave birth to a baby saucepan for your profit. Why is it so difficult for you to believe that a pot can die when the loss falls upon you? Whatever has the power to be born must surely have the nature to pass away!'

Kasim stood frozen on the doorstep, utterly speechless. His own foolish greed had trapped him completely. The surrounding neighbors who had gathered to listen burst into uncontrollable laughter at Kasim's humiliation. Kasim slunk back into his house in shame, cured forever of taking advantage of others through greedy loopholes.
moral: 道德启示：You cannot accept an absurd claim when it profits you, and then reject it when it costs you. Greed blinds people to truth and exposes them to poetic justice.

title: Puss in Boots and the Gift of Loyalty (简体中文)
summary: When a poor miller's son inherits only a small tomcat, the clever cat asks for a pair of leather boots and uses ingenuity and loyalty to transform his master's fortune. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
Once upon a time, an old miller died and left all his earthly possessions to his three sons. The eldest received the flour mill, the second received the donkey, and the youngest son, Julien, received only the family tomcat.

Julien was heartbroken. 'My brothers can join together and earn an honest living,' he sighed, 'but what can I do with a cat? Once I feed him, I shall starve!'

The cat, who was dozing by the fire, stood up on his hind legs, arched his back, and spoke in a refined, courteous voice: 'Do not despair, good master! You possess far greater wealth than you realize. Only grant me a sturdy pair of leather boots and a canvas sack with drawstrings, and you will see that your inheritance is not as meager as you believe.'

Julien was astonished, but remembering the cat's remarkable cunning at catching mice, he spent his last few coins to commission a cobbler to craft a handsome pair of leather boots. The cat pulled on the boots with great pride, slung the sack over his shoulder, and strode out into the morning meadow like a gallant nobleman.

First, Puss in Boots went to a grassy warren. He filled the sack with sweet bran and clover, laid it open upon the grass, and played dead. Soon, a plump young rabbit hopped inside to nibble the clover. Puss swiftly pulled the drawstrings tight! Instead of eating the rabbit himself, Puss marched straight to the King's royal palace.

Bowing low before the throne, Puss announced: 'Sire, I present you with this wild rabbit, sent with deep respect from my noble lord, the Marquess of Carabas' (a grand title Puss invented on the spot for his master).

The King was delighted and thanked the courteous cat. Over the next two months, Puss regularly brought partridges and fresh game to the palace, always presenting them as gifts from the Marquess of Carabas.

One sunny afternoon, knowing that the King and his daughter—the most kind-hearted princess in the realm—would be riding in their royal coach along the riverbank, Puss sprinted to his master: 'Quick! Take off your clothes and bathe in the river, and leave the rest to me!'

Julien obeyed. As the King's golden carriage rolled past, Puss ran to the roadside screaming at the top of his lungs: 'Help! Help! The Marquess of Carabas is drowning! Thieves have stolen his clothes!'

The King recognized the famous cat and ordered his royal guards to rescue the young man. The King opened his royal wardrobe trunk and presented Julien with a splendid suit of embroidered silk and a feathered velvet hat. When Julien stepped forward, tall, handsome, and naturally polite, the princess smiled warmly, and the King invited him to ride inside the royal coach.

Puss sprinted ahead. Coming upon meadows where farmers were mowing hay, Puss called out: 'Good people, tell the King that these meadows belong to the Marquess of Carabas, or you shall face trouble!' When the carriage passed, the happy farmers cheered that the lush lands belonged to the generous Marquess.

Finally, Puss reached a magnificent stone castle belonging to a wealthy ogre who possessed the magical power of shape-shifting. Puss walked boldly into the great hall and bowed: 'Great lord, I have heard it said that you can transform into any creature at will, even a roaring lion!'

'Indeed I can!' roared the boastful ogre. In a flash, he transformed into a terrifying lion with golden fangs. Puss scrambled up the curtains in fright!

When the ogre returned to his normal shape, Puss bowed again: 'Magnificent! But surely it is impossible for one so colossal to turn into a creature as tiny as a mouse? That would be too difficult even for you.'

'Impossible? Watch this!' scoffed the vain ogre. Instantly, the ogre transformed into a tiny brown mouse scampering across the stone floor. Puss leaped like lightning, pounced upon the mouse, and that was the end of the ogre's tyranny!

When the King's carriage arrived at the castle gates, Puss opened the doors wide: 'Welcome, Your Majesty, to the castle of my master, the Marquess of Carabas!'

The King was enchanted by Julien's modesty, kindness, and fine castle. Seeing that Julien and the princess had fallen in love with mutual admiration, the King gave his blessing for their marriage. Julien never forgot that his happiness was born from loyalty, and Puss in Boots became a great lord, chasing mice only for recreation on sunny afternoons.
moral: 道德启示：Resourcefulness, loyalty, and courtesy are more valuable than mere inherited wealth. A clever and faithful companion can turn hardship into triumph.
