title: The Four Scholars and the Forest Lion (简体中文)
summary: From Tantra 5 (Apariksitakarakam 5.3), four young friends set out to seek fortune. Three possess vast scholarly book-learning but lack practical common sense, while the fourth has simple good judgment, teaching that wisdom is far superior to mere erudition. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
In a town of northern India lived four young friends. Three of them—named Vidvatta, Shastrika, and Grantha—had spent years studying in prestigious academies. They had mastered ancient grammar, scientific formulae, logic, and obscure lore, but were puffed up with intellectual vanity and completely devoid of common sense.

The fourth friend, named Subuddhi, had not studied advanced scholarly books, but possessed keen observation, practical wisdom, and deep common sense.

One day, the three scholarly friends decided to travel to royal courts to win fame and gold. At first, they sneered at Subuddhi: 'Why should we take him? He has no formal academic degrees!' But remembering their childhood friendship, they agreed to let Subuddhi join them.

While walking through a dense, shadowy forest, the four companions came upon a pile of dry, bleached bones scattered beneath a tall banyan tree.

The first scholar, Vidvatta, beamed with pride: 'Look! Here is an opportunity to prove the power of our learning! These are the bones of a dead beast. I have mastered the secret science of assembling bones into their exact skeletal anatomy!' He recited a formula, and the bones flew together, forming the complete skeleton of a colossal lion!

The second scholar, Shastrika, stepped forward: 'I can supply the flesh, blood, skin, organs, and golden mane!' He recited a second formula, and immediately red muscles, golden fur, sharp fangs, and claws enveloped the skeleton. A complete, terrifying lion lay upon the leaves, looking as if it were merely asleep.

The third scholar, Grantha, raised his hands eagerly: 'Now watch my supreme genius! I possess the secret art of breathing life into the dead! I shall awaken this lion!'

Subuddhi looked at the giant predator with growing alarm. He grabbed Grantha's arm and whispered urgently: 'Stop, my brother! For heaven's sake, do not do it! That is a ferocious, carnivorous mountain lion! If you give it life, its first instinct will be to pounce upon us and tear us to pieces!'

The scholar shook off Subuddhi's hand with disdain: 'Stand aside, you uneducated simpleton! Will you stop me from demonstrating my academic greatness?'

'If you insist on bringing it to life,' replied Subuddhi calmly, 'grant me just ten seconds to climb this tall banyan tree before you speak your words!'

Subuddhi scrambled nimbly up the sturdy trunk of the banyan tree and perched securely on a high, leafy branch.

The third scholar laughed and recited his formula. The lion's chest rose and fell. Its golden eyes opened, glowing with feral hunger. The beast let out a thunderous roar that shook the forest leaves, leaped forward upon the three scholars who had created it, and chased them through the thickets, giving them the fright of their lives and a lesson they would never forget, while sensible Subuddhi climbed down peacefully after the predator had galloped away, walking safely back to his village.
moral: 道德启示：Common sense is far superior to mere book-learning. Knowledge without wisdom, caution, and practical judgment can become the instrument of your own undoing.

title: The Dreamer and the Broken Pot of Flour (简体中文)
summary: From Tantra 5 (Apariksitakarakam 5.7), a daydreaming villager hangs a clay pot of barley flour above his bed and spins wild fantasies of trading and wealth, until an energetic daydream kick shatters everything into dust. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
keywords: building castles in the air fable
full_text:
In a quiet village of ancient India lived a man named Svabhavakripana. He had a gentle heart, but was notoriously fond of sitting on his porch, daydreaming for hours instead of putting his hands to honest work.

One afternoon, as charity for assisting in a harvest festival, a merchant gave him a large earthen jar completely filled with fine, white barley flour. Svabhavakripana carried the heavy jar home with great joy. To protect the precious flour from mice and ants, he tied a strong rope around the neck of the pot, suspended it securely from a peg directly above his woven sleeping cot, and lay down beneath it, gazing up at the jar.

As the afternoon breeze whispered through the window, Svabhavakripana's imagination took flight:

*'Behold this magnificent jar of barley flour!'* he thought with a grin. *'If a famine strikes the land next month, the price of flour will soar! I shall sell this single jar for one hundred silver coins! With those hundred silver coins, I shall buy two healthy she-goats. In six months, the goats will give birth, and within two years, I shall have a herd of fifty goats!'*

He smiled wider, turning on his side: *'Then I shall sell the herd of goats and purchase twenty milk cows! The cows will give rich milk and calves. In five years, I shall sell the cows and buy a herd of royal mares, becoming the greatest horse merchant in the province!'*

Svabhavakripana's eyes sparkled in his trance: *'With the wealth from my horses, I shall build a magnificent four-story palace with marble fountains and fragrant gardens. A wealthy nobleman will arrive and offer his daughter's hand in marriage, and we shall have a handsome baby boy!'*

He drifted deeper into the daydream: *'One day, when my son is playing in the palace courtyard, he will crawl too close to the horse stables. I shall call out to my wife: "Quick, take the child inside!" But suppose she is busy in the kitchen and does not hear me? I shall become so angry that I will run forward and give her a furious kick like this!'*

Caught completely in the grip of his vivid fantasy, Svabhavakripana lashed out with his right foot in real life with all his strength! *WHACK!*

His foot struck the earthen pot hanging directly above his bed. The clay jar shattered into a hundred jagged pieces, and ten pounds of powdery white barley flour rained down directly upon his face, hair, eyes, and bed, completely covering him in white dust like a ghost!

Svabhavakripana sat up in his dusty bed, sputtering, coughing, and rubbing flour from his eyes. His great herd of goats, his dairy cows, his royal stallions, his marble palace, and his family had vanished into thin air—leaving him with nothing but a broken clay pot and a dirty floor to sweep!

The neighbors heard the crash and peered through the window. Seeing Svabhavakripana looking like a white flour monster, they burst into hearty laughter. Svabhavakripana bowed his head in shame, having learned that dreaming without doing real work is like building castles out of powdery dust.
moral: 道德启示：Do not build castles in the air or rely on fantasies of the future. Success requires practical effort, hard work, and living in the reality of today.

title: The Crows and the Black Snake (简体中文)
summary: A pair of devoted crows outsmart a greedy black snake living in the hollow of their banyan tree by using royal jewelry to lead the palace guards to its lair. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
High in the sturdy branches of a great banyan tree on the outskirts of an ancient city, a pair of devoted crows had built their nest. Season after season, they tended their home with gentle care, watching the seasons turn from sweltering summer to the lush green of the monsoon.

Yet deep within the hollow at the base of the very same tree lived a long, venomous black snake. Each time the mother crow laid a clutch of speckled eggs, the snake slithered silently up the trunk while the parents were away foraging and devoured the nestlings.

Heartbroken and weeping bitter tears, the mother crow turned to her mate. "My dear husband, we cannot bear this sorrow another season. We must abandon our banyan tree and fly away to a distant forest where our children will be safe."

The father crow shook his head thoughtfully. "This ancient banyan has sheltered our family for generations. We should not surrender our home in despair before we have tried the power of counsel. Brute force we lack, but wisdom is a weapon greater than fangs. Let us visit our neighbor, the old jackal who lives near the riverbank. He has seen many winters and understands the ways of the world."

The two crows flew to the riverbank and sat beside the wise jackal, pouring out their grief. The jackal listened intently, his amber eyes reflecting the golden light of the setting sun.

"Do not weep, dear friends," the jackal said softly. "The strong may crush by sheer weight, but the clever can guide the strong to do their work for them. Tell me, do the queen and her maidens still bathe every morning in the calm waters of the lake near the king's palace?"

"They do," replied the father crow. "Every morning at dawn, surrounded by armed guards."

"Then your path is clear," the jackal smiled. "Tomorrow morning, wait until the queen removes her precious necklace of pearls and gold and lays it upon the stone pavilion on the shore. Swoop down boldly, seize the glittering chain in your beak, and fly slowly—not too fast, so the guards may keep you in sight. Fly straight toward your banyan tree, drop the necklace directly into the dark hollow where the snake sleeps, and watch from the highest branches."

The crows thanked their wise friend and waited eagerly for dawn.

As the morning mist lifted, Queen Priyamvada and her maidens arrived at the lake. Taking off her magnificent pearl necklace, she placed it upon a silk cushion on the stone steps before stepping into the water. In a sudden rush of black wings, the father crow descended, snatched the sparkling necklace in his beak, and let out a loud caw.

"Thief! A crow has stolen the queen's royal jewels!" cried the palace guards, raising their spears and racing across the meadow after the flying bird.

The crow flew steadily, pausing on low branches to ensure the breathless guards stayed close behind. When he reached the great banyan tree, he circled the trunk, hovered over the hollow at its roots, and dropped the shimmering pearl necklace deep inside.

Arriving at the foot of the tree, the royal guards peered into the dark crevice. Seeing the glint of pearls, a soldier reached down with a staff. Instantly, the enraged black snake hissed furiously and reared its hooded head to strike.

Defending themselves against the venomous serpent, the soldiers struck it with their spears until the danger was ended. They retrieved the queen's necklace unharmed and hurried back to the palace with their duty fulfilled.

From the highest branch, the crows watched their tree become peaceful and safe once more. They raised their young in joyful security, knowing that clear thought and clever planning could overcome even the most dangerous foe.
moral: 道德启示：Intelligence and careful planning can overcome brute force and seemingly impossible obstacles.

title: The Sparrow, the Woodpecker, the Fly and the Frog (简体中文)
summary: When a reckless, stomping elephant destroys a tiny sparrow's nest, four small forest creatures unite their unique talents to teach the giant creature a lesson in humility. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
In a quiet glade of a flowering sal forest, a pair of humble sparrows had built their soft grass nest on a low, sheltered bough. They took gentle pride in their humble shelter, and soon four tiny chicks chirped sweetly under their mother's warm wings.

One hot afternoon, a massive bull elephant named Dantamalla charged through the forest in a frenzy of wild pride. He tore branches from trees, trampled bushes underfoot, and trumpeted with arrogant defiance. Reaching the sal tree, the elephant seized the sturdy bough with his trunk and snapped it with a deafening crack.

The nest tumbled into the dust. Though the parent sparrows fluttered frantically into the sky, their fragile home was crushed beneath the elephant's heavy strides as he strode away without a backward glance.

The mother sparrow settled on a fallen twig, weeping inconsolably. Her shrill cries drew the attention of her dear friend, a woodpecker named Wood-Borer.

"Why do you weep so bitterly, sister sparrow?" asked the woodpecker gently.

"A reckless giant of an elephant has crushed my home in his senseless arrogance," wept the sparrow. "He believes that because he is enormous and we are tiny, our lives and homes have no value. If no one checks his pride, he will destroy every nest in the forest!"

The woodpecker nodded solemnly. "Grief alone will not restore what is lost, but united effort can establish justice. Let us visit my friend, the blue fly named Sharp-Ear. She has sharp senses and a swift flight."

Together, the sparrow and woodpecker visited the blue fly, who was filled with indignation upon hearing of the tragedy. "Brute strength cannot withstand coordinated action," said the fly. "Let us also consult the elderly frog, Cloud-Voice, who leads the amphibian council by the reed marsh."

Beside the calm waters of the lotus marsh, Old Cloud-Voice listened thoughtfully. "No single creature among us can match the elephant's raw bulk," the wise frog croaked, "yet each of us possesses a unique gift that the giant lacks. If we combine our abilities in sequence, we can gently guide this wanderer to the muddy clay pit where his pride will be cooled."

The four friends agreed upon a clever plan.

At noon, when the sun blazed hottest, Sharp-Ear the fly buzzed softly near the drowsy elephant's ears, singing a hypnotic, melodious humming song. Intrigued and relaxed by the soothing tune, Dantamalla closed his heavy eyes to listen.

At that instant, Wood-Borer the woodpecker tapped gently at the dry twigs nearby, startling the elephant so that he blinked and stepped backward, feeling disoriented in the glaring heat.

Parched with thirst from the blistering afternoon, the elephant strained his ears to find water. Deep in the canyon where a safe, shallow clay pool lay bordered by soft marsh grass, Old Cloud-Voice and hundreds of his frog brethren began to croak in unison: "Croak! Croak! Water is here!"

Hearing the familiar chorus of frogs, the thirsty elephant believed a great, cool lake lay ahead. He rushed down the grassy slope and plunged feet-first into the thick, sticky riverbed clay.

The elephant sank up to his knees in the safe, squelching mud. Try as he might, his massive weight held him firmly pinned, unable to advance or rampage.

From the surrounding trees, the tiny sparrow, woodpecker, fly, and frog gathered. 

"Dantamalla," spoke the mother sparrow in a clear, resonant voice. "Look at us. We are the smallest creatures in this woodland, yet together we have brought your rampaging feet to a standstill. Your great tusks and heavy steps gave you power, but power without compassion brings harm to all."

Humbled and exhausted, the elephant bowed his massive head in the cool mud. "I have acted foolishly and blinded myself with arrogance," he rumbled with genuine sorrow. "Forgive me, little ones. From this day forward, I shall walk through the forest with care, respecting every leaf, every branch, and every humble home."

The woodland creatures guided the village foresters to help haul the elephant safely free using thick hemp ropes, and from that day on, Dantamalla walked the sal forest as a gentle guardian of all creatures great and small.
moral: 道德启示：Even the smallest and humblest individuals can accomplish great deeds when they unite their strengths in harmony.

title: The Two-Headed Bharunda Bird (简体中文)
summary: A mythical bird with two heads sharing one stomach learns the tragic consequence of petty jealousy and selfish rivalry. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
Along the sunlit shores of a vast ocean lived a wondrous bird named Bharunda. Nature had endowed this magnificent creature with a unique form: it possessed two distinct heads, each with its own sharp eyes and curved beak, yet both heads were joined to a single sturdy body and shared a single stomach.

For many years, the two heads lived in peaceful companionship. When the left head looked toward the sapphire sea, the right head surveyed the emerald jungle. When the left head slept in the shade, the right head stayed alert, keeping watch against forest predators. They shared every joy and every flight above the billowing clouds.

One balmy afternoon, while strolling along the golden sand, the first head spotted a rare and luscious fruit fallen from the legendary Amrita tree. Its skin glowed with the color of ripe apricots, and its fragrance was sweeter than fresh honeycomb.

With a joyful cry, the first head scooped the fruit in its beak and began to savor its luscious sweetness. "Oh, how divine!" exclaimed the first head. "Never in all my days have I tasted anything so rich, fragrant, and delightful!"

The second head leaned down, its eyes gleaming with curiosity. "Brother, pray grant me a morsel! Let me taste this wondrous fruit with my own beak so that I too may experience its sweetness on my tongue."

The first head puffed up its feathers selfishly. "Why should you waste time tasting it with your beak? Have you forgotten our nature? We share one neck, one throat, and one single stomach. When I swallow this delicious fruit, its nourishment and strength will enter our common body just the same. Therefore, it makes no difference which beak enjoys the taste!"

With that, the greedy first head swallowed the remainder of the nectar-sweet fruit in one swift gulp, licking its beak with smug satisfaction.

The second head felt deeply wounded and insulted by this selfish dismissal. It said nothing aloud, but resentment took root in its heart. "He cared only for his own tongue's fleeting pleasure, ignoring our sacred partnership," the second head brooded silently. "He forgot that what hurts one inevitably affects both."

A few days later, while pecking among the rocky crags at the base of the cliffs, the second head noticed a dark, bitter fruit hanging from a poisonous creeping vine. Its stench was sharp and foul.

The second head bent low, about to seize the noxious berry in its beak.

Horrified, the first head shrieked, "Stop, brother! Do not touch that fruit! That is the deadly berry of the poison vine. If you swallow it, its venom will enter our bloodstream and our common body will perish!"

The second head glared with bitter defiance. "A few days ago, you proclaimed that it matters not which head eats, for both are fed by the same stomach. Now it is my turn to choose what enters our shared stomach! I shall eat this berry, if only to prove that you cannot trample my feelings without consequence!"

"Have you lost your mind?" cried the first head in terror. "A grudge is not worth our very life! Forgive my thoughtless greed, and let us live!"

Seeing the genuine remorse and terror in the first head's eyes, the second head hesitated with its beak inches above the poisonous fruit. The cool ocean breeze swept over their shared wings, carrying the sweet scent of the forest they both loved so dearly.

The second head let the bitter fruit drop onto the stony ground and kicked it far into the swirling waves below.

"You were foolish and selfish," whispered the second head quietly, "and in my anger, I was prepared to destroy us both just to win an argument. How blind we become when pride and spite govern our thoughts."

The first head bowed low against the second head, rubbing their feathered cheeks together in deep contrition. "Never again shall I hoard a joy for myself, for we are bound as one."

From that day forth, whenever the Bharunda bird found a berry, a seed, or a sweet fig, the two heads took turns sharing every bite, proving that unity thrives only when nurtured by mutual respect and generous hearts.
moral: 道德启示：Selfishness and petty revenge within a shared partnership lead only to mutual destruction.

title: The King of the Mice and the Elephant Herd (简体中文)
summary: A community of mice asks a majestic herd of elephants to take a different path to the lake; later, when the elephants are trapped in hunters' ropes, the mice repay the kindness. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
In an ancient, forgotten city whose sandstone temples had long crumbled into quiet mounds of wild jasmine, a vast community of mice had established a peaceful kingdom. Beneath the flagstones and hollow marble pillars, thousands of little rodents lived in warmth and harmony, digging cozy burrows and gathering wild millet.

Not far from this ancient ruin lay a shimmering lake bordered by tall bamboo groves. One summer, when a prolonged drought dried up the surrounding pools, a great herd of elephants led by their wise king, Gajendra, journeyed toward the lake to drink.

As the herd thundered across the ruined city, their colossal feet unknowingly crushed hundreds of mouse burrows, causing panic and distress throughout the subterranean halls.

The elders of the mouse clan gathered in solemn council. "If the elephant herd marches through our city every day to reach the lake, our underground homes will be destroyed," said the mice.

Hiranyaka, the brave and articulate king of the mice, stepped forward. "Great creatures often act without malice simply because they cannot see what lies beneath their feet. Let us go directly to King Gajendra and speak with courtesy and truth."

Scurrying along the forest trail, Hiranyaka climbed upon a mossy boulder right before the towering elephant monarch. Standing upon his hind legs, the mouse bowed politely and addressed the giant.

"O noble king of the forest," squeaked Hiranyaka clearly, "I am Hiranyaka, sovereign of the mouse folk dwelling in the old city. When your mighty herd passes through our ruins, your heavy steps crush our burrows. We know you mean no harm, but we ask of your noble heart: would you graciously take the path that winds around the eastern ridge instead? If you show us this mercy, a day may come when we humble mice may return your kindness."

The younger elephants in the herd snickered in disbelief. "How could tiny creatures who fit inside our footprints ever help a mighty herd of elephants?" they laughed.

But King Gajendra was wise and honorable. He silenced the mockers with a wave of his majestic trunk. He looked down upon the tiny mouse king with respect.

"Noble Hiranyaka," said the elephant king kindly. "Every life is precious, and strength should protect rather than destroy. We shall gladly use the eastern trail from this day forward. Keep your city in peace."

Months passed, and the monsoon rains filled the forest with verdant life. One evening, a group of royal trappers arrived from the capital, spreading heavy hemp nets and thick braided ropes through the forest trails. When Gajendra and his herd walked down to the water, they became ensnared in the cunningly concealed snares.

Try as they might, the powerful elephants could not break free from the thick, knotted cords. The more they pulled, the tighter the ropes bound their legs. The forest echoed with their anxious trumpeting.

Hearing the distress calls from afar, Hiranyaka recognized the voice of King Gajendra. "Our benefactor is in peril!" shouted the mouse king. "Rally every family! Every sharp tooth must work tonight!"

Thousands of mice hurried across the moonlit glade like a silver wave. Reaching the trapped elephants, Hiranyaka called out, "Be calm, noble king! Your small friends have arrived!"

The mice swarmed over the thick hemp cords. With their razor-sharp incisors, thousands of little teeth gnawed through the heavy strands. Strand by strand, knot by knot, the thick ropes fell away in shredded fibers.

Within an hour, every elephant in the herd was completely free, well before the trappers returned at dawn.

King Gajendra lifted Hiranyaka gently with his trunk and placed him lovingly upon his broad forehead. "Forgive those among us who doubted you," the elephant king rumbled with deep gratitude. "Tonight we learned that a true friend, no matter how small, is a treasure beyond compare."

From that night onward, the elephant herd and the mouse kingdom lived in unbreakable alliance, each looking out for the other across the changing seasons.
moral: 道德启示：Kindness is never wasted; even the smallest friend may prove to be of the greatest help in times of need.

title: The Brahmin and the Three Rogues (简体中文)
summary: Three cunning tricksters conspire to trick a scholar into abandoning a healthy goat by repeatedly insisting it is an unclean dog. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
In a quiet village nestled in the foothills lived an honest scholar named Mitra Sharma. He was well-versed in ancient texts and respected for his learning, yet he had one peculiar weakness: he cared deeply about what others said and was easily swayed by repeated opinions.

One auspicious autumn morning, Mitra Sharma performed a ceremonial blessing for a wealthy landowner in a neighboring hamlet. In gratitude, the generous host gifted the scholar a plump, healthy young goat with sleek white fur.

Delighted with the gift, Mitra Sharma hoisted the quiet goat gently across his broad shoulders and set off on foot along the dusty high road back to his home village.

Along the same road, three lazy rogues were sitting under the shade of a tamarind tree, having spent their day without earning a single copper coin. Seeing the scholar approaching with a fine, healthy animal, their eyes lit up with mischief and greed.

"Look at that plump goat!" whispered the first rogue. "If we could obtain it, what a grand feast we could prepare tonight!"

"He is strong and holds it securely," muttered the second. "We cannot overpower him without raising the alarm."

"Force is the weapon of fools," smiled the third rogue cunningly. "Let us employ psychology. People believe what they hear repeated by many voices. We shall position ourselves along the road at separate intervals and each tell him the exact same unbelievable tale. Watch how quickly doubt conquers knowledge."

The three tricksters separated quickly.

Mitra Sharma walked merrily along, humming a peaceful melody, when the first rogue stepped out from behind a hedge. The rogue bowed low and feigned utter astonishment.

"Greetings, revered scholar!" cried the man, covering his mouth in theatrical disgust. "Pardon my boldness, but why is a dignified scholar carrying an unclean, mangy stray dog upon his sacred shoulders?"

Mitra Sharma frowned with annoyance. "Are you blind, fellow? Can you not distinguish between a plump white goat and a stray dog? Open your eyes before you speak nonsense!"

The first rogue shrugged apologetically. "Be not angry, sir. If you choose to carry a dog, that is your affair. I only spoke what my eyes witnessed." He walked away with a knowing chuckle.

Mitra Sharma shook his head, adjusted the goat on his shoulders, and walked on. Yet a faint seed of bewilderment had been planted in his thoughts.

Half a mile further along the winding trail, the second rogue emerged from a grove of mango trees. Stopping in his tracks, he gasped in dramatic shock.

"Heavens preserve us!" shouted the second rogue. "Revered pandit, what strange vow has compelled a holy man of your stature to carry a dead calf upon his back in broad daylight? The whole village will mock you!"

Mitra Sharma turned pale with indignation. "What madness has gripped travelers today? This is no calf! It is a living, breathing young goat gifted to me this very morning!"

"Sir, there is no need to shout at me," replied the rogue calmly. "Touch its ears and feel its hooves. If you cannot tell a dead calf from a goat, pray do not blame honest passersby!" And he strolled off, shaking his head in pity.

Now Mitra Sharma felt genuine anxiety gnawing at his stomach. He set the goat down upon the road, looked into its gentle eyes, stroked its fleece, and felt its tiny horns. "It certainly looks like a goat, feels like a goat, and bleats like a goat," he muttered to himself. "Yet two independent travelers have seen something entirely different. Could a demon have bewitched this creature?"

Reluctantly, he lifted the goat once more and walked with hesitant, cautious steps.

Near the crossroads entering his home village, the third rogue was leaning against a milestone. As the scholar drew near, the rogue burst into loud, mocking laughter.

"Look at the village scholar!" the man shouted to the empty fields. "He carries a donkey on his back instead of riding it! What a comical sight!"

That was the final straw. Mitra Sharma's confidence shattered completely.

"Three different strangers in three different places cannot all be mistaken!" gasped the terrified scholar. "This creature is truly a shape-shifting goblin that transforms into a dog, a calf, and a donkey to deceive travelers! If I carry it into my home, it will bring ruin upon my household!"

In a blind panic, Mitra Sharma dropped the goat into the road, lifted the hem of his robe, and ran as fast as his legs could carry him all the way to his house, bolting his front door behind him.

The three rogues emerged from their hiding places, embraced each other with roar of laughter, and led the gentle white goat away to enjoy their ill-gotten prize.
moral: 道德启示：Do not let repeated rumors or peer pressure make you doubt what you know to be true with your own senses.

title: The Cave That Talked Back (简体中文)
summary: When a ravenous lion hides inside a jackal's cave, the quick-witted jackal asks the cave why it has not welcomed him home as usual, exposing the predator's presence. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
In a dense jungle surrounded by rocky cliffs lived an aging lion named Kharanakhara. Though he possessed mighty claws and a thunderous roar, his joints had grown stiff with age, making it difficult for him to chase swift deer across the open plains.

One evening, after hunting all day without catching a single meal, the famished lion stumbled upon a large, inviting cave dug into the side of a sandstone bluff.

Peering inside, the lion saw that the cave was clean, cozy, and clearly inhabited by some forest animal. "Whoever lives here is sure to return at sunset to sleep," thought the lion, his stomach rumbling. "I shall slip inside, hide silently in the darkest corner, and feast when the owner steps through the entrance."

The lion crept inside and crouched low behind a rocky ledge, holding his breath and keeping his golden eyes fixed on the entrance.

The cave belonged to a shrewd and observant jackal named Dadhipuccha. As twilight deepened and the stars began to twinkle in the purple sky, the jackal trotted toward his home, looking forward to a restful night.

Reaching the mouth of the cave, the jackal stopped abruptly. His keen eyes noticed large, deep paw prints pressed into the soft sand, leading straight into the dark cavern.

He looked around carefully. There were clear footprints going in, but not a single footprint leading out.

"Danger lurks within," the jackal thought to himself, his heart beating fast. "A great predator has entered my home and is waiting to ambush me. If I enter blindly, I am doomed. Yet if I run away without being certain, I may abandon my warm cave over a false alarm. I must devise a test that forces the intruder to reveal himself without putting me in harm's way."

Standing at a safe distance from the entrance, well out of pouncing range, the jackal cleared his throat and shouted loudly toward the dark opening:

"O Cave! Greetings, my wonderful Cave! O Cave! Why do you maintain such an icy silence tonight?"

Inside the darkness, the lion held his breath, wondering what was happening.

Receiving no reply, the jackal raised his voice even louder: "O beloved Cave! Have you forgotten the solemn covenant we made long ago? Did you not promise that every evening when I return from foraging, you would call out a warm greeting to welcome me home, and only then would I enter? If you refuse to speak to me tonight as you always do, I shall turn around right now and find shelter in another cave!"

Crouched in the shadows, the hungry lion became anxious. "Aha!" thought the foolish lion. "This cave must indeed speak aloud to welcome the jackal every evening! It must be silent right now only because it is terrified of my royal presence. If the cave does not reply, the jackal will walk away and my dinner will escape! I must answer in place of the cave!"

Clearing his throat, the lion threw back his mane and roared from the depths of his belly: "WELCOME HOME, DEAR JACKAL! ENTER FREELY AND REST!"

The lion's massive roar echoed off the stone walls like a thunderclap, shaking the dust from the ceiling and echoing for miles across the quiet forest. Several birds flew from the trees in panic.

Outside, the jackal chuckled softly, shaking his head at the lion's gullibility.

"O foolish king of the forest!" called out the jackal merrily. "Since the dawn of creation, who has ever heard of a cave made of stone that speaks with a living voice? Thank you for warning me with your own roar!"

With a joyful leap, the clever jackal bounded away into the moonlit forest, leaving the hungry lion to wait in the empty cave with nothing but an empty stomach and bruised pride.
moral: 道德启示：Presence of mind and quick wit can rescue you from the most dangerous traps.

title: The Donkey in the Tiger's Skin (简体中文)
summary: A washerman drapes an old tiger skin over his thin donkey so it can graze freely in villagers' cornfields, but the donkey's sudden bray reveals his true identity. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
In a quiet village beside a sparkling river lived a poor washerman named Shuddhapata. He owned an old gray donkey who had served him faithfully for many years, carrying heavy bundles of laundry between the village huts and the washing ghats.

As winter set in, fodder became scarce, and the poor donkey grew so emaciated that his ribs could be counted beneath his gray coat. The washerman loved his beast of burden and grieved to see him hungry, yet he lacked the money to purchase oats or hay.

One afternoon, while collecting firewood in the forest, the washerman discovered the dried skin of a royal Bengal tiger that had perished of natural old age. The striped pelt was intact, with ferocious whiskers and gleaming markings.

An ingenious, mischievous idea flashed into the washerman's mind. "If I drape this magnificent tiger skin over my poor donkey at twilight and lead him into the rich barley and cornfields belonging to the neighboring farmers, the watchmen will flee in terror believing a wild beast has descended from the hills! My donkey can feast to his heart's content, and no one will dare lay a hand upon him!"

That evening, the washerman carefully draped the tiger skin over the donkey, securing it snugly beneath his belly. He led the disguised creature to the edge of a lush, emerald-green barley field and let him loose.

Seeing the striped silhouette moving gracefully through the tall crops, the field watchmen shrieked in horror. "A royal tiger has invaded the village fields! Save yourselves!" Dropping their bamboo torches and wooden staves, the watchmen scrambled to safety and locked themselves inside their stone watchtowers.

For hours, the donkey feasted upon the tender, sweet barley shoots. His belly grew plump and round, his sunken eyes regained their sparkle, and his strength returned. Before dawn, the washerman led him quietly back home and removed the pelt.

This nightly deception continued for several weeks. The donkey grew sleek, strong, and vigorous, while the terrified farmers kept their distance, whispering legends about the mysterious tiger that devoured only barley and tender wheat.

One moonlight night, while the disguised donkey was grazing contentedly in a distant pasture, the faint, resonant bray of another donkey echoed across the valley from a neighboring farm: "Hee-haw! Hee-haw!"

Hearing the familiar music of his own kind, the donkey's ears pricked up with uncontrollable excitement. His heart swelled with joy. For weeks he had maintained complete silence, suppressing his natural voice beneath the heavy tiger fur.

Unable to restrain himself a moment longer, the donkey threw back his head, lifted his tail, and unleashed his loudest, most joyful bray: "HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW! HEE-HAW!"

Up in the stone watchtower, the shivering farmers froze. They looked at each other in utter bewilderment.

"Listen!" whispered an old farmer. "Does a royal tiger bray like an ass?"

"That is no tiger at all!" shouted another watchman, rubbing his eyes in anger. "That is merely a washerman's donkey draped in a tiger's pelt! He has fooled us for a month and devoured our finest harvest!"

Armed with sturdy wooden sticks, the farmers rushed down from the tower. Hearing the shouting, the foolish donkey tried to run, but the heavy pelt slipped around his hooves, tripping him up.

The farmers chased the imposter out of the field, giving him a sound scolding with their sticks until he galloped all the way back to the washerman's courtyard, thoroughly cured of playing the role of a ferocious beast.

From that night forward, the donkey was content to graze on simple grass by the riverbank, having learned that wearing another's skin can never change who you truly are inside.
moral: 道德启示：Fine clothes and false appearances can deceive for a moment, but words and actions will always reveal your true nature.

title: Hundred-Wit, Thousand-Wit, and Single-Wit (简体中文)
summary: Two proud fish boasting of hundreds of escape strategies hesitate when fishermen arrive, while a humble frog with one simple plan saves himself immediately. [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
keywords: hundred wit thousand wit single wit
full_text:
In a tranquil, lotus-dappled pond tucked away in a verdant valley lived two splendid fish and a humble frog who had formed a close companionship.

The first fish was named Shatabuddhi, which means "Owner of a Hundred Wits." He had dazzling silver scales, long flowing fins, and an immense pride in his intellectual abilities.

The second fish was named Sahasrabuddhi, which means "Master of a Thousand Wits." His golden scales shimmered in the sunlight, and he claimed to have studied every current, eddy, and escape maneuver known to aquatic life.

The frog was named Ekabuddhi, meaning "Possessor of a Single Wit." He was a modest green frog with bumpy skin, who made no pretense of great learning, relying instead upon simple observation and clear common sense.

Every afternoon, the three friends gathered beside a submerged mossy rock to discuss the affairs of the pond, the change in the tides, and the wisdom of the world.

One golden evening at sunset, as the three friends conversed, two fishermen carrying heavy woven nets and wicker baskets walked along the pond's grassy bank.

One fisherman pointed at the clear water. "Look, brother! This secluded pond is teeming with large, plump fish! Tomorrow morning at dawn, we shall return with our finest drag-nets and harvest every fish in this water."

"Agreed," replied his companion. "We shall bring the weighted nets and leave not a single pool unsearched."

The two fishermen continued on their way toward the village.

Trembling with fear, Ekabuddhi the frog turned to his two fish companions. "Friends! Did you hear what those fishermen said? They will return at the break of dawn with deadly nets! Our pond is in mortal peril. What shall we do? Should we flee tonight through the narrow stream that connects our pond to the great river?"

Shatabuddhi, the fish of a hundred wits, laughed smoothly and flicked his tail with disdain. "Calm yourself, my dear little frog! Do not panic over mere words spoken by passing men. The world is full of boastful talk that comes to nothing. Even if they return with nets, I possess a hundred clever maneuvers. I can dart through the reeds, bury myself in the silt, or jump over the floats. I shall easily save us all!"

Sahasrabuddhi, the fish of a thousand wits, swelled his gills proudly. "Your hundred wits are commendable, brother, but my thousand wits are supreme! I know the ancient arts of swimming backward, twisting in figure-eights, and feigning death so that fishermen toss you back. Fleeing our ancestral home over a rumor is beneath our dignity. Stay put and rely on our superior intellect!"

Ekabuddhi the frog listened thoughtfully to their grand speeches. He looked at the darkening sky, then at the shallow exit stream whose waters were already beginning to drop.

"Dear friends," said the humble frog gently. "You have hundreds and thousands of wits, but I have only one simple wit. And my single wit tells me that when danger announces its arrival for dawn, the only sensible choice is to be somewhere else when dawn arrives."

That very evening, before the moon rose high, Ekabuddhi called his wife and little tadpoles. Swimming quietly through the shallow outlet stream, the frog family migrated to a deep, safe river well beyond the fishermen's reach.

At dawn, as the morning mist hovered over the lotus pond, the fishermen arrived carrying their massive, weighted drag-nets. They cast the heavy cords into the water, sweeping from bank to bank.

Shatabuddhi attempted his hundred clever maneuvers: he darted left, dived into the weeds, and twisted against the mesh, but the fine netting caught him securely. Sahasrabuddhi deployed his thousand intricate swimming patterns, but the heavy lead weights pinned the net firmly to the pond floor.

Both proud fish were hauled ashore in the fishermen's overflowing basket.

Sitting safely upon a lily pad in the great river, Ekabuddhi watched the fishermen pass along the distant road, carrying their heavy load toward the market.

"Intellect and knowledge are wonderful gifts," murmured the frog to his children, "yet when danger approaches, a single ounce of decisive action is worth more than a thousand brilliant theories left untested."
moral: 道德启示：Simple common sense and timely, decisive action are far more valuable than overthinking and boastful theories.

Then Caliph Harun al-Rashid in disguise with Jafar and banishmenter Masrur knocks, also admitted.

Ladies beat dogs and weep, beat lutes. Porter and guests ask meaning. Ladies explain their histories: first lady was beaten by demon, second lady's tale, portress tale. Kalandars tell their tales. Caliph reveals himself and marries sisters.

full_text: Sindbad the Landsman, poor porter, complains of fate before rich Sindbad the Seaman's house. title: The Fox and the Grapes (简体中文)
summary: A Fox one day spied a beautiful bunch of ripe grapes hanging from a vine trained along the branches of a tree. The grapes seemed ready to burst with juice, and the Fox's mouth watered as he gazed... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
A Fox one day spied a beautiful bunch of ripe grapes hanging from a vine trained along the branches of a tree. The grapes seemed ready to burst with juice, and the Fox's mouth watered as he gazed longingly at them. The bunch hung from a high branch, and the Fox had to jump for it. The first time he jumped he failed to reach it. So he walked a short distance and took a running leap at it, only to fall short once more.

Again and again he tried, but in vain. Now he sat down and looked at the grapes in disgust. 'What a fool I am,' he said. 'Here I am wearing myself out to get a bunch of sour grapes that are not worth gaping for.' And off he went. Moral: It is easy to despise what you cannot get.

title: The Tortoise and the Hare (简体中文)
summary: A Hare was making fun of the Tortoise one day for being so slow. 'Do you ever get anywhere?' he asked with a mocking laugh. 'Yes,' replied the Tortoise, 'and I get there sooner than you think.... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
A Hare was making fun of the Tortoise one day for being so slow. 'Do you ever get anywhere?' he asked with a mocking laugh. 'Yes,' replied the Tortoise, 'and I get there sooner than you think. I'll run you a race and prove it.' The Hare was much amused at the idea of running a race with the Tortoise, but for the fun of the thing he agreed. So the Fox, who had consented to act as judge, marked the distance and started the runners off.

The Hare was soon far out of sight, and to make the Tortoise feel very deeply how ridiculous it was for him to try a race with a Hare, he lay down beside the course to take a nap until the Tortoise should catch up. The Tortoise meanwhile kept going slowly but steadily, and, after a time, passed the place where the Hare was sleeping. But the Hare slept on very peacefully; and when at last he did wake up, the Tortoise was near the goal. The Hare now ran his swiftest, but he could not overtake the Tortoise in time. Moral: Slow and steady wins the race.
moral: 道德启示：Slow and steady wins the race.

title: The Ant and the Grasshopper (简体中文)
summary: In a field one summer's day a Grasshopper was hopping about, chirping and singing to its heart's content. An Ant passed by, bearing along with great toil an ear of corn he was taking to the nest.... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
In a field one summer's day a Grasshopper was hopping about, chirping and singing to its heart's content. An Ant passed by, bearing along with great toil an ear of corn he was taking to the nest. 'Why not come and chat with me,' said the Grasshopper, 'instead of toiling and moiling in that way?' 'I am helping to lay up food for the winter,' said the Ant, 'and recommend you to do the same.' 'Why bother about winter?' said the Grasshopper; 'we have got plenty of food at present.' But the Ant went on its way and continued its toil.

When the winter came the Grasshopper had no food and found itself dying of hunger, while it saw the ants distributing every day corn and grain from the stores they had collected in the summer. Then the Grasshopper knew: It is best to prepare for days of need. Moral: Work today for tomorrow.

summary: Once when a Lion was asleep a little Mouse began running up and down upon him; this soon wakened the Lion, who placed his huge paw upon him, and opened his big jaws to swallow him. 'Pardon, O... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]

Once when a Lion was asleep a little Mouse began running up and down upon him; this soon wakened the Lion, who placed his huge paw upon him, and opened his big jaws to swallow him. 'Pardon, O King,' cried the little Mouse: 'forgive me this time, I shall never forget it: who knows but what I may be able to do you a turn some of these days?' The Lion was so tickled at the idea of the Mouse being able to help him, that he lifted up his paw and let him go. Some time after the Lion was caught in a trap, and the hunters who desired to carry him alive to the King, tied him to a tree while they went in search of a wagon to carry him on.

Just then the little Mouse happened to pass by, and seeing the sad plight in which the Lion was, went up to him and soon gnawed away the ropes that bound the King of the Beasts. 'Was I not right?' said the little Mouse. Moral: Little friends may prove great friends.

title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf (简体中文)
summary: There once was a shepherd boy who was bored as he sat on the hillside watching the village sheep. To amuse himself he took a great breath and sang out, 'Wolf! Wolf! The Wolf is chasing the sheep!'... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
There once was a shepherd boy who was bored as he sat on the hillside watching the village sheep. To amuse himself he took a great breath and sang out, 'Wolf! Wolf! The Wolf is chasing the sheep!' The villagers came running up the hill to help the boy drive the wolf away. But when they arrived at the top of the hill, they found no wolf. The boy laughed at the sight of their angry faces. 'Don't cry wolf, shepherd boy,' said the villagers, 'when there's no wolf!' They went grumbling back down the hill. Later, the boy sang out again, 'Wolf! Wolf! The wolf is chasing the sheep!' To his naughty delight, he watched the villagers run up the hill to help him drive the wolf away. When the villagers saw no wolf they sternly said, 'Save your frightened song for when there is really something wrong! Don't cry wolf when there is no wolf!' But the boy just grinned and watched them go grumbling down the hill once more.

Later, he saw a REAL wolf prowling about his flock. Alarmed, he leaped to his feet and sang out as loudly as he could, 'Wolf! Wolf!' But the villagers thought he was trying to fool them again, and so they didn't come. At sunset, the villagers wondered why the shepherd boy hadn't returned with their sheep. They went up the hill to find the boy. They found him weeping. 'There really was a wolf here! The flock has scattered! I cried out, Wolf! Why didn't you come?' An old man tried to comfort the boy as they went to bring back the sheep. 'We'll help you look for the lost sheep in the morning,' he said, putting his arm around the youth, 'Nobody believes a liar...even when he is telling the truth!' Moral: Liars are not believed even when they speak the truth.

title: The Crow and the Pitcher (简体中文)
summary: A Crow, half-dead with thirst, came upon a Pitcher which had once been full of water; but when the Crow put its beak into the mouth of the Pitcher he found that only a very little water was left... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
A Crow, half-dead with thirst, came upon a Pitcher which had once been full of water; but when the Crow put its beak into the mouth of the Pitcher he found that only a very little water was left in it, and that he could not reach far enough down to get at it. He tried, and he tried, but at last had to give up in despair. Then a thought came to him, and he took a pebble and dropped it into the Pitcher. Then he took another pebble and dropped it into the Pitcher.

Then he took another pebble and dropped that into the Pitcher. Then he took another pebble and dropped that into the Pitcher. At last, at last, he saw the water mount up near him, and after casting in a few more pebbles he was able to quench his thirst and save his life. Moral: Little by little does the trick.

title: The Fox and the Crow (简体中文)
summary: A Fox once saw a Crow fly off with a piece of cheese in its beak and settle on a branch of a tree. 'That's for me, as I am a Fox,' said Master Reynard, and he walked up to the foot of the tree.... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
A Fox once saw a Crow fly off with a piece of cheese in its beak and settle on a branch of a tree. 'That's for me, as I am a Fox,' said Master Reynard, and he walked up to the foot of the tree. 'Good day, Mistress Crow,' he cried. 'How well you are looking today: how glossy your feathers; how bright your eye.

I feel sure your voice must surpass that of other birds, just as your figure does; let me hear but one song from you that I may greet you as the Queen of Birds.' The Crow lifted up her head and began to caw her best, but the moment she opened her mouth the piece of cheese fell to the ground, only to be snapped up by Master Fox. 'That will do,' said he. 'That was all I wanted. In exchange for your cheese I will give you a piece of advice for the future: Do not trust flatterers.' Moral: Do not trust flatterers.

full_text:
There was once a Countryman who possessed the most wonderful Goose you can imagine, for every day when he visited the nest, the Goose had laid a beautiful, glittering, golden egg. The Countryman took the eggs to market and soon began to get rich. But it was not long before he grew impatient with the Goose because she gave him only a single golden egg a day. He was not getting rich fast enough.

Then one day, after he had finished counting his money, the idea came to him that he could get all the golden eggs at once by killing the Goose and cutting it open. But when the deed was done, not a single golden egg did he find, and his precious Goose was dead. Moral: Those who have plenty want more and so lose all they have.

full_text:
The Wind and the Sun were disputing which was the stronger. Suddenly they saw a traveller coming down the road, and the Sun said: 'I see a way to decide our dispute. Whichever of us can cause that traveller to take off his cloak shall be regarded as the stronger. You begin.' So the Sun retired behind a cloud, and the Wind began to blow as hard as it could upon the traveller.

But the harder he blew the more closely did the traveller wrap his cloak round him, till at last the Wind had to give up in despair. Then the Sun came out and shone in all his glory upon the traveller, who soon found it too hot to walk with his cloak on. Moral: Kindness effects more than severity.

full_text:
Once upon a time a Wolf resolved to disguise his appearance in order to secure food more easily. Encased in the skin of a sheep, he pastured with the flock deceiving the shepherd by his costume.

In the evening he was shut up by the shepherd in the fold; the night and the fold were both dark, and the shepherd, on his return to the fold, instantly vanquished the Wolf, mistaking him for a sheep. Moral: Harm seek, harm find.

title: Yeh-Shen (Ye Xian) - China - Oldest Known Cinderella (简体中文)
summary: In ancient China, Chief Wu had two wives. One died leaving daughter Yeh-Shen, beautiful and clever at pottery. Her stepmother hated her and made her work in caves gathering firewood and water.... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
keywords: yeh-shen (ye xian) - china - oldest known cinderella
full_text:
In ancient China, Chief Wu had two wives. One died leaving daughter Yeh-Shen, beautiful and clever at pottery. Her stepmother hated her and made her work in caves gathering firewood and water. Yeh-Shen had only one friend, a fish with golden eyes in a pond, which she fed daily. Stepmother discovered fish, defeated it and ate it, hiding bones. An old man from heaven told Yeh-Shen to hide fish bones in her room; whatever she wished would be granted. New Year festival came, stepmother forced her to stay home. Yeh-Shen prayed to bones and was given a cloak of kingfisher feathers and tiny golden slippers.

She went to festival, charmed all, but fled losing one slipper when step-siblings chased. A trader from To'han found slipper and presented to king. King searched for owner, trying slipper on all women. Finally Yeh-Shen tried it, it fit perfectly. She wore feather cloak again, king married her. Stepmother and stepsister were banished from the kingdom? Actually they fled and were buried in flying stones in some versions.
moral: 道德启示：Wisdom, patience, and kind conduct lead to peace and happiness.

full_text:
A gentleman's daughter after mother's death suffers under second wife with two proud daughters. She is made to sleep in attic among cinders, called Cinderella (Cendrillon). Father in her shadow. Prince holds ball for two days. Cinderella weeps, her fairy godmother appears, transforms pumpkin into carriage, mice into horses, rat into coachman, lizards into footmen, her rags into beautiful gown of cloth of gold and silver, gives glass slippers (pantoufle de verre - some say vair fur).

Warns to leave before midnight when magic ends. Cinderella goes, charms prince, leaves at midnight first night, second night stays till clock strikes twelve, loses glass slipper fleeing. Prince proclaims he will marry woman who fits glass slipper. Stepsisters try to force foot, fail. Cinderella asks to try, fits, produces second slipper, fairy godmother makes her even more beautiful, marries prince, forgives stepsisters and marries them to lords.

title: Aschenputtel - Germany - Brothers Grimm (简体中文)
summary: A rich man's wife dies, tells daughter to remain pious. Man remarries woman with two daughters beautiful but evil. They call stepdaughter Aschenputtel (Ashputtel) because she must sit in ashes.... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
A rich man's wife dies, tells daughter to remain pious. Man remarries woman with two daughters beautiful but evil. They call stepdaughter Aschenputtel (Ashputtel) because she must sit in ashes. Father goes to fair, asks what to bring, stepdaughters ask fine clothes, Aschenputtel asks first branch that knocks his hat on way home. Father brings hazel branch, she plants on mother's grave, waters with tears, grows into great tree, white bird lives in it granting wishes. King holds three-day festival to find bride. Aschenputtel asks stepmother to go, denied, stepmother throws lentils into ashes task.

White birds sort lentils. Aschenputtel goes to tree: 'Shiver and quiver little tree, silver and gold throw down over me.' Bird throws gold and silver dress and silk slippers. She goes to ball, prince dances only with her, she escapes. Three nights, dresses more beautiful each night, third night prince spreads pitch, loses gold slipper. Prince goes house to house, stepsisters cut toe and heel to fit, doves cry 'Rook di goo, blood in shoe!' Finally Aschenputtel fits, doves say she is true bride. At wedding, doves peck out stepsisters' eyes for wickedness.
moral: 道德启示：Wisdom, patience, and kind conduct lead to peace and happiness.

full_text:
Far out in the ocean, where the water is as blue as the prettiest cornflower and as clear as crystal, it is very deep. There dwell the Sea King and his subjects. The Sea King's palace is made of coral. His old mother keeps house, proud of noble birth, with six sea-princesses, youngest the Little Mermaid, with beautiful voice. She is 15, may rise to surface. She sees prince on ship, storm sinks ship, she saves prince, falls in love.

She visits Sea Witch who lives in creepy forest of polyps, gives her voice in exchange for human legs, each step feels like walking on knives. She drinks potion, tail becomes legs, but mute. Prince finds her, loves her as child but loves another princess he thinks saved him. Little Mermaid has chance to kill prince with knife given by sisters who traded hair to witch, to become mermaid again. She cannot, throws knife, throws herself into sea, becomes foam, but becomes daughter of air, earning soul after 300 years of good deeds. Moral on selfless love.

Devil made magic mirror that makes beautiful look ugly. Goblins break it, splinters fly into eyes and hearts making people cold. Kay and Gerda are friends. Splinter enters Kay's eye and heart, he becomes cold, mocks Gerda. Snow Queen, beautiful woman of ice and snow, kisses Kay (two kisses make forget Gerda, third would kill), takes him to palace in Lapland.

Gerda searches: talks to river, old woman who combs hair with magic, crows, robber girl with knife, Lapland woman and Finland woman. Finmark, finds Kay in Snow Queen palace trying to spell 'Eternity' with ice pieces, but cannot. Gerda weeps, tears melt heart, removes splinter, Kay weeps removing eye splinter. They return home, now grown-ups, but children in heart.

full_text:
Far out in the ocean, where the water is as blue as the prettiest cornflower and as clear as crystal, it is very deep. There dwell the Sea King and his subjects. The Sea King's palace is made of coral. His old mother keeps house, proud of noble birth, with six sea-princesses, youngest the Little Mermaid, with beautiful voice. She is 15, may rise to surface. She sees prince on ship, storm sinks ship, she saves prince, falls in love.

She visits Sea Witch who lives in creepy forest of polyps, gives her voice in exchange for human legs, each step feels like walking on knives. She drinks potion, tail becomes legs, but mute. Prince finds her, loves her as child but loves another princess he thinks saved him. Little Mermaid has chance to kill prince with knife given by sisters who traded hair to witch, to become mermaid again. She cannot, throws knife, throws herself into sea, becomes foam, but becomes daughter of air, earning soul after 300 years of good deeds. Moral on selfless love.

full_text:
Far out in the ocean, where the water is as blue as the prettiest cornflower and as clear as crystal, it is very deep. There dwell the Sea King and his subjects. The Sea King's palace is made of coral. His old mother keeps house, proud of noble birth, with six sea-princesses, youngest the Little Mermaid, with beautiful voice. She is 15, may rise to surface. She sees prince on ship, storm sinks ship, she saves prince, falls in love.

She visits Sea Witch who lives in creepy forest of polyps, gives her voice in exchange for human legs, each step feels like walking on knives. She drinks potion, tail becomes legs, but mute. Prince finds her, loves her as child but loves another princess he thinks saved him. Little Mermaid has chance to kill prince with knife given by sisters who traded hair to witch, to become mermaid again. She cannot, throws knife, throws herself into sea, becomes foam, but becomes daughter of air, earning soul after 300 years of good deeds. Moral on selfless love.

full_text:
Far out in the ocean, where the water is as blue as the prettiest cornflower and as clear as crystal, it is very deep. There dwell the Sea King and his subjects. The Sea King's palace is made of coral. His old mother keeps house, proud of noble birth, with six sea-princesses, youngest the Little Mermaid, with beautiful voice. She is 15, may rise to surface. She sees prince on ship, storm sinks ship, she saves prince, falls in love.

She visits Sea Witch who lives in creepy forest of polyps, gives her voice in exchange for human legs, each step feels like walking on knives. She drinks potion, tail becomes legs, but mute. Prince finds her, loves her as child but loves another princess he thinks saved him. Little Mermaid has chance to kill prince with knife given by sisters who traded hair to witch, to become mermaid again. She cannot, throws knife, throws herself into sea, becomes foam, but becomes daughter of air, earning soul after 300 years of good deeds. Moral on selfless love.

title: Vessantara Jataka - The Prince Who Gave Everything (简体中文)
summary: Vessantara, last birth before Buddha, was prince renowned for generosity. He had magic elephant that brings rain, gave it to enemy kingdom suffering drought. People angry, king Vessantara's father... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
keywords: vessantara jataka - the prince who gave everything
full_text:
Vessantara, last birth before Buddha, was prince renowned for generosity. He had magic elephant that brings rain, gave it to enemy kingdom suffering drought. People angry, king Vessantara's father banishes him. Vessantara leaves with wife Maddi and two children Jali and Kanhajina. On way gives away carriage, horses. Lives in Vamka mountain hermitage. Brahmin Jujaka, cruel old man, asks for children as servants.

Vessantara gives children, though heart breaks, as ultimate Dana Paramita perfection of generosity. Sakka as the king of clouds tests him asking for wife Maddi, he gives. Sakka returns wife. Jujaka brings children to city, grandfather King Sanjaya ransoms grandchildren, Jujaka dies overeating. Vessantara returns as king. This Jataka taught for centuries, illustrates perfect charity. Moral: Supreme generosity leads to Buddhahood.
moral: 道德启示：Paramita perfection - Dana, Sila, Kshanti etc.

title: Chaddanta Jataka - Six-Tusked Elephant (简体中文)
summary: Bodhisatta born as Chaddanta, chief of 8000 elephants, six-tusked white elephant, with two wives Mahasubhadda and Cullasubhadda. Cullasubhadda jealous of Mahasubhadda. She prays to be queen in... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
Bodhisatta born as Chaddanta, chief of 8000 elephants, six-tusked white elephant, with two wives Mahasubhadda and Cullasubhadda. Cullasubhadda jealous of Mahasubhadda. She prays to be queen in next life to kill Chaddanta. Reborn as queen of Benares, feigns illness, says only six-tusked elephant tusks will cure. King sends hunter Sonuttara, who after 7 years finds Chaddanta.

Chaddanta, seeing hunter tired, feeds him. Hunter shoots Chaddanta with poison arrow. Chaddanta, though dying, helps hunter cut tusks, not angry, forgives queen. Queen sees tusks, realizes his forgiveness, dies of remorse. Moral: Forgiveness even to murderer - Kshanti Paramita.
moral: 道德启示：Paramita perfection - Dana, Sila, Kshanti etc.

title: Nigrodha Jataka - Banyan Deer (简体中文)
summary: Bodhisatta born as Banyan Deer King, golden deer with herd of 500, rival herd Sakha with 500. King of Benares hunts daily. Deer kings agree to send one deer daily by lot to king's kitchen to avoid... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
Bodhisatta born as Banyan Deer King, golden deer with herd of 500, rival herd Sakha with 500. King of Benares hunts daily. Deer kings agree to send one deer daily by lot to king's kitchen to avoid whole herd slaughter. One day lot falls on pregnant doe in Sakha's herd, she begs Sakha, Sakha refuses, she goes to Bodhisatta Banyan deer. Bodhisatta says 'Go, I will go in your place.' Bodhisatta goes to banishment block.

Cook sees golden deer, reports king. King asks why. Banyan deer speaks: 'I came for doe.' King moved by sacrifice, spares all deer, grants abhaya dana - safety to all animals. Moral: Compassionate king self-sacrifice.
moral: 道德启示：Paramita perfection - Dana, Sila, Kshanti etc.

title: Vessantara - Last of Ten Great Jatakas (简体中文)
summary: Vessantara, last birth before Buddha, was prince renowned for generosity. He had magic elephant that brings rain, gave it to enemy kingdom suffering drought. People angry, king Vessantara's father... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
keywords: vessantara - last of ten great jatakas
full_text:
Vessantara, last birth before Buddha, was prince renowned for generosity. He had magic elephant that brings rain, gave it to enemy kingdom suffering drought. People angry, king Vessantara's father banishes him. Vessantara leaves with wife Maddi and two children Jali and Kanhajina. On way gives away carriage, horses. Lives in Vamka mountain hermitage. Brahmin Jujaka, cruel old man, asks for children as servants.

Vessantara gives children, though heart breaks, as ultimate Dana Paramita perfection of generosity. Sakka as the king of clouds tests him asking for wife Maddi, he gives. Sakka returns wife. Jujaka brings children to city, grandfather King Sanjaya ransoms grandchildren, Jujaka dies overeating. Vessantara returns as king. This Jataka taught for centuries, illustrates perfect charity. Moral: Supreme generosity leads to Buddhahood.
moral: 道德启示：Paramita perfection - Dana, Sila, Kshanti etc.

title: Sivi Jataka - King Sivi Gives Eyes (简体中文)
summary: King Sibi (Sivi) famous for self-sacrifice. the king of clouds as hawk and Agni as dove test him. Dove flies to Sibi's lap seeking refuge from hawk. Hawk says 'Dove is my food, give me.' Sibi says 'I must... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
keywords: sivi jataka - king sivi gives eyes
full_text:
King Sibi (Sivi) famous for self-sacrifice. the king of clouds as hawk and Agni as dove test him. Dove flies to Sibi's lap seeking refuge from hawk. Hawk says 'Dove is my food, give me.' Sibi says 'I must protect refugee.' Hawk: 'Then give equal weight of your flesh.' Sibi cuts flesh from thigh, puts on scale, dove always heavier.

Finally Sibi himself sits on scale giving whole body. Gods reveal themselves, heal him, bless. Moral: King protects even small creature at cost of self.

title: Sasa Jataka - The Hare and Moon (简体中文)
summary: Once Bodhisatta was born as a hare. He lived with monkey, jackal, otter. They decided to keep Uposatha fast. A Brahmin (Sakka in disguise) came begging food. Monkey gave mangoes, otter fish,... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
keywords: sasa jataka - the hare and moon
full_text:
Once Bodhisatta was born as a hare. He lived with monkey, jackal, otter. They decided to keep Uposatha fast. A Brahmin (Sakka in disguise) came begging food. Monkey gave mangoes, otter fish, jackal stolen meat, but hare had only grass which Brahmin cannot eat.

So hare said 'Use me as food' and jumped into fire. Sakka revealed himself, did not let hare burn, took hare and painted his image on moon for all to see. Hence moon has hare. Moral: Perfect self-sacrifice Dana Paramita.
moral: 道德启示：Paramita perfection - Dana, Sila, Kshanti etc.

title: Sivi Jataka variant (简体中文)

full_text:
King Sibi (Sivi) famous for self-sacrifice. the king of clouds as hawk and Agni as dove test him. Dove flies to Sibi's lap seeking refuge from hawk. Hawk says 'Dove is my food, give me.' Sibi says 'I must protect refugee.' Hawk: 'Then give equal weight of your flesh.' Sibi cuts flesh from thigh, puts on scale, dove always heavier.

Finally Sibi himself sits on scale giving whole body. Gods reveal themselves, heal him, bless. Moral: King protects even small creature at cost of self.
moral: 道德启示：Paramita perfection - Dana, Sila, Kshanti etc.

title: The Wedge-Pulling Monkey (简体中文)
summary: A merchant was building a temple near his town. The carpenters working there went to eat, leaving a log half-split with a wedge in it. A troop of monkeys came playing. One foolish monkey, whose... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
A merchant was building a temple near his town. The carpenters working there went to eat, leaving a log half-split with a wedge in it. A troop of monkeys came playing. One foolish monkey, whose death was near, sat on the log and began pulling at the wedge, saying 'What is this in the wrong place?' His tail and paws were caught in the cleft.

When he pulled the wedge out, the log closed and he was trapped until the carpenters returned. Moral: The fool who meddles in what he does not understand comes to grief. This is what happens when you interfere in others' work.
moral: 道德启示：Wisdom, patience, and kind conduct lead to peace and happiness.

summary: A starving jackal named Gomaya wandered into a battlefield and found nothing but a war-drum left behind. The wind blew and a creeper struck the drum: 'Boom!' The jackal was terrified, then... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
A starving jackal named Gomaya wandered into a battlefield and found nothing but a war-drum left behind. The wind blew and a creeper struck the drum: 'Boom!' The jackal was terrified, then thought: what makes this sound must be full of food. He crept closer and found only wood and skin.

He tore it open and found it empty. He said to himself: I thought this big noise had much inside, but it is nothing. So a loud boaster may be empty inside.

title: Shell-Neck Slim and Grim (简体中文)
summary: Turtle Shell-Neck and two geese Slim and Grim were friends. Drought came. Geese decided to move to another lake, carrying turtle on a stick held in beaks, turtle holding middle with mouth, warned... [简体中文 ಆವೃತ್ತಿ / பதிப்பு / संस्करण]
full_text:
